What was done to carry out the recommendations of the committee on Agriculture and Colonization in regard to granting reduced rates for the transport of Canadian settlers and with reference to the advantages which were to be given to sons of Canadian farmers haying a knowledge of agriculture in order to facilitate their settling on the land?

The report of the select standing committee on agriculture and colonization recommended on June 6, 1928, that " measures be taken to ascertain whether the railways will restore the homeseekers' rates in effect prior to the war, making such rates effective eastbound as well as westbound." Id accordance with this recommendation a letter, dated July 7, 1928, was addressed to the presidents of the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian National railways by the Deputy Minister of Immigration and Colonization, calling their attention to the recommendation of the select standing committee and inquiring if the railways would restore the homeseekers' rates. All the railways in Canada being concerned, the matter was referred by the presidents to the Canadian Passenger Association which subsequently replied as follows:-
*Referring to your letter of July 7th addressed to the presidents of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways quoting an extract from report of the select standing committee on agriculture and colonization advocating the restoration of home seekers' rates in effect prior to the war, making such rates effective east-bound as well as westbound.
As this is a matter that affects all Canadian railways to a more or less extent, it has been referred to the Canadian Passenger Association for consideration and reply.
Specially low fares for home seekers from eastern to western Canada were inaugurated, as you will probably recollect, many years ago when it was difficult to secure settlers for the prairie provinces and it was necessary from a national standpoint to encourage the movement in every way possible. At that time there was very little business and commercial travel oetween the east and west.
As the settlement of the western provinces ,/rogressed, business and commercial travel gradually developed and the home seekers' travel from eastern Canada steadily decreased. As the legitimate use of the fare gradually [Mr. Forke.l
diminished, the railways in order to protect their interests against the advantage being taken of the fare by business and commercial travel gradually raised the charge.
The increase in home seekers' fares has not been detrimental in so far as settlement of the west is concerned, inasmuch as the exceptionally ow harvest help fares authorized each year meet the requirements of the actual land seeker from eastern Canada far better than the home se -kers' excursion fares, which is evidenced by th fact that for a number of years the majority of those in eastern Canada who desir 'd to settle on the land in the west took advantage of these special harvest help fares. This gives them the advantage of working for farmers in the west and earning more than enough to pay their passage fares both ways, and those who decide to settle in the western n ovinces arrange to move their families at the time of the next harvest excursion, when tli v have their buildings and home under way air1 ready to receive them.
Further, we are of the opinion that present conditions in Canada are such as to make it inadvisable to unduly encourage removal of individuals and families from one province to another. All provinces have vacant land and are anxiously endeavouring to not only hold their present population but to secure new settlers. Certain of the provinces have even felt the drain caused by the harvesters' excursions and have made protest against the arrangement. Our records indicate that from fifteen to twenty per cent of the harvesters who go west each year do not return to the east and that the majority of those who do not return actually settle on the land.
After very careful consideration the railways are strongly of the opinion that it would not be in the general interest to make any reduction in the present so-called "homeseekers' fares".
The select standing committee also recommended, subject to the completion of satisfactory arrangements with governments of the provinces, that assistance equal to that given by the British government to British emigrant boys be extended by the government of Canada to the Canadian youth who are trained in agriculture. This is still the subject of negotiation with the provincial governments.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION

speechtext:
The house resumed, from February 21, consideration of the proposed motion of Mr Church:
That, in the opinion of this house, immediate action should be taken, without further and unnecessary delays, to enter into a treaty with the government of the United States for the immediate development and generation of waterpower on the St. Lawrence river and its deepening and development in the interests of navigation, and that a great St. Lawrence waterway is an immediate and economic necessity for the welfare and best interests of Canada.
And that this house is further of the opinion that the government should undertake the construction and operation of this canal as a public undertaking itself and the power incident herein should be developed and generated at cost by the government for the people under public ownership and not alienated to private interests for gain or exported for use outside Canada.
He said:	This particular resolution calls
for a national federal policy regarding the St. Lawrence waterway, a policy such as was given to Ontario in light and power in this matter by Sir James Whitney and Sir Adam Beck.

There would have been no hydro-electric movement in Ontario had it not been for the Conservative party. It was this policy of Whitney and Beck that did so much for the industries of the province of Ontario, and made it the great agricultural province it is to-day, by giving cheap power and light to the farmer, the labourer, and the housewife in the urban centres of population.
The particular St. Lawrence waterway proposition before us has been under discussion and has stood the test of investigation by committees of advisory engineers for ten years. They have made their report, and the Conservative party, if in power, would have no difficulty whatever in solving this problem. There is, I admit, a little division in our own party on this question, between our friends from Quebec and our friends from Ontario, but I predict a solution will be had that under our honoured leader (Mr. Bennett), who has given his life to public service, and has spent his best years in service for others and for the good of the country generally. There is no district in the province of Ontario where the name of Hon. R. B. Bennett is more honoured and stands higher or more respected by everybody and by all classes of citizens than in Toronto.
The Conservative party would have no difficulty in solving this problem were they in offioe. So far as I am concerned, I make no apology about saying I have always been a Whitney-Beck Conservative. I have stood for the preservation of our water-powers for the people all the time, and I would like to see the Conservative party in this Dominion take up the development of the St. Lawrence waterway and make it a plank in the Conservative party platform. The country owes everything of a constructive nature to the Conservative party. It is the party which the country always sends for when in trouble. The Liberal-Conservative party founded the hydro-electric system in the face of the opposition of the Ross-Hardy government. I warn this government to be very careful in what it does with respect to water-power, because in 1905 the Ross-Hardy government in Ontario was defeated at the polls and driven from office by people of all parties in the province of Ontario because of the iniquitous power deals they had made. To-day in the city of Winnipeg the Bracken government is on its last legs over the question of the Seven Sisters falls. A year ago the Beauharnois boys very nearly got away with the title deeds of power in the St. Lawrence waterway, from this government in power here at Ottawa, and then we would have had, the' St. Lawrence

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Chwch
waterway. Last session I asked for papers to be brought down to parliament dealing with the Seven Sisters question, but the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) asked me to let my motion stand, and the result was that the proper papers have never been brought down at all. I advise the government to go slow in regard to the Beauharnois project. Let them look at Winnipeg and see what is happening there over cheap light and power. The people of Canada are in no mood to put up with this giving away of the title deeds to our natural resources.
The Conservative party was responsible for the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway. It is the party that is responsible for the policy of protection. It has always been a consistent constructive party, and has always been ready to risk unpopularity to stand by its principles. It is the Conservative party that is to-day developing the Pacific coast province, where the Liberal administration was recently defeated at the polls. The Conservative party at present in Ontario has given the province the best administration it has ever had in the various departments since confederation. We now have honesty of administration. The different public departments in the province were never so well run as they are to-day. We have never had such progressive administration in the province in the matter of public health, good roads, education or research. There is only one matter in which I differ from the government of the province, and that is they have given up the policy of Sir Adam Beck, and are failing to generate and distribute the power and have become just a purchaser of power. No public enterprise ever encountered the venom and experienced more unfair and unjust misrepresentation than did the work of the HydroElectric Power Commision of Ontario, and now the St. Lawrence waterway has to encounter the same kind of opposition. But the hydro-electric power commission became the chief glory of the Liberal-Conservative party in Ontario, headed by Sir James Whitney and Sir Adam Beck.
The country always sends for the Conservative part in time of national difficulty and when great economic problems have to be solved. If any government ever made a football of a great economic problem it is the present government in its treatment of the St. Lawrence waterway. They talk about a division of opinion in the Conservative party with respect to the proper solution of this question; but that is nothing compared with the lack of harmony among hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to the same question. This government no longer represents the true principles of Liberalism. Sir James Whitney and
Sir Adam Beck, when they founded the hydro, had to face all kinds of opposition, abuse and obstruction. They were even called amateur anarchists, and the opponents of the hydro in the press and in the elections did everything to ridicule the Niagara and Chippawa power projects
Lord Kelvin was called in to advise regarding the possibility of bringing power from DeCew falls to Hamilton, thirty-eight miles. Apparently he could not see very far, for he said that if they put their money in the Welland canal they could dredge the canal and might get it back, but if they put their money in the proposed DeCew falls development they would never get it back. Amid such doubts and fears Sir Adam Beck went ahead and overcame all opposition and, backed up by the hydro Conservatives, he made hydro development in Ontario the sucess it is today as a means of cheap light and power. The government and its Beauharnois friends will have the battle of their lives on their hands if they try to alienate the sovereign rights of the province of Ontario in the water-powers of the St. Lawrence and the water-powers of Ontario. These are the property of the people, and they must be developed for the benefit of the people. It was the people's money that demonstrated the worth of waterpower development in Ontario, and there can be no greater dereliction of duty on the part of those who are departing from that basic principle under the bogey of a temporary saving by buying power instead of developing it, a saving which in years to come will cost the people of this province tens of millions of dollars. There should have been no departure from that basic policy of Sir Adam Beck.
In the Beauharnois company the people of Canada are threatened by a monopoly more powerful than Canada has ever seen, and should the water-powers of the St. Lawrence be turned over to that company, generations yet unborn will be adversely affected in their economic and industrial development, and in their domestic life. In parting with these water-powers we are in effect placing a huge debt on future generations and mortgaging the profits of their labour.
As the Ontario government has apparently changed its hydro policy, and has revoked Sir Adam Beck's program of developing and generating power, becoming thereby a mere customer or purchaser of power from the electric monopoly in Quebec, the federal government has a great opportunity to come out with a federal hydro policy. And it is not outside the British North America Act for the federal authorities to develop and generate power from
412	COMMONS
St. Laurence Waterway-Mr. Church
canal works and distribute the current at cost to the provinces. This would make for a greater Canada.
The national advisory committee appointed by the government reported on the St. Lawrence project as follows:
1.	That the project is practical, necessary and urgent;
2.	There is no fear of United States aggression, or loss of sovereign rights;
3.	It involves no further cost to the Dominion government or the taxpayer;
4.	That it will be of incalculable benefit in navigation and power;
5.	The entire project is an economic desire that should be immediately accomplished.
This report goes on to show the utter economic absurdity of an all-Canadian canal. An all-Canadian canal is not feasible from the standpoint of navigation, power or diversion of water, and the country could not afford it. The sovereignty bogey is raised by the private power interests to enable them to grab the people's heritage. They talk about the American bogey while various Ontario governments have conceded in economic ways to the Americans more territory than did King George III. Prom the Ottawa river to the Nipigon, in the vast hinterland of new Ontario, the timber, the pulpwood, the mines and the water-powers have been ceded to American promoters for a few paltry dollars.
I believe the time has come when the Conservative party should take up this St. Lawrence waterway question. They should close their ranks and try to solve this vital problem for the benefit of the central provinces of Canada. That used to be the attitude of the Ontario government. I heard Mr. Ferguson on platforms all over Ontario supporting that policy of a greater St. Lawrence waterway. If they have since revoked Sir Adam Beck's program I shall be much surprised, because it will hurt the Conservative party in Ontario which has always been the champion of the great public ownership policy in Ontario under which hydro-electric development has been made such an outstanding success. The Conservatives did it all and deserve the credit. The municipalities of Ontario now have nearly $300,000,000 invested in that development in light, power and transportation. The city of Toronto has an investment of nearly $100,000,000, and it is my duty to protect that investment, and I will continue to protect it. If the Ontario government have become a mere customer of the great electric monopoly in Quebec, then the federal government has a unique oppor-
tunity to proclaim a federal hydro policy. As I have already said, such a policy is not outside the British North America Act. What is wanted is a national and federal canal policy, and a national and federal hydro policy, as applied to the St. Lawrence. This would be the salvation of Canada and the making of any party that undertakes it in the open.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution of the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) might more appropriately be termed a series of resolutions. With the permission of the house I will re-read his motion:
That, in the opinion of this house, immediate action should be taken, without further and unnecessary delays, to enter into a treaty with the government of the United States for the "'.mediate development and generation of waterpower on the St. Lawrence river and its deepening and development in the interests of navigation. and that a great St. Lawrence waterway is an immediate and economic necessity for the welfare and best interests of Canada.
And that this house is further of the opinion that the government should undertake the coni' iction and operation of this canal as a public undertaking itself and the power incident herein should be developed and generated at cost by the government for the people under public ownership and not alienated to private interests for gain or exported for use outside Canada.
The house will observe that the motion asks, first of all, that a treaty be entered into immediately with the United States for the development and generation of waterpower on the, St. Lawrence. That is the first proposal; it is with respect to waterpower. The second is that a treaty be entered into immediately with the United States for the deepening and development of the St. Lawrence river in the interests of navigation. The third proposal is that the house declare that a great St. Lawrence waterway is an immediate and economic necessity for the welfare and best interests of Canada. In the fourth place, the resolution proposes that the government of Canada should undertake the construction and operation of this canal as a public enterprise. The resolution does not say what canal is meant, whether it is some canal, which is to be ancilliary to the St. Lawrence river, or whether it is the channel of the St. Lawrence when deepened. Then there is a fifth proposal, that the power incidental to the canal-that is, either the supplementary canal or the deepened channel of the St. Lawrence-should be developed and generated by the government at cost. There is a sixth proposal, that the power incidental to the canal should be developed under public ownership and not as a private undertaking.

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Mackenzie King
And, finally, there is the recommendation that the power incidental to the canal should not be exported for use outside of Canada.
There are seven different propositions on which the house is .called upon to pronounce an a single resolution. I direct the attention of the house to this immediately, because it is important that all parties interested should understand the reason which may govern the house should it decline to accept the resolution in the form in which it has been presented. It is not a single resolution; rather, as I have said, it is a bill of fare, and I am inclined to think contains too many items to admit of proper digestion at a single session of parliament.
I would invite my hon. friend's attention to the step which was taken early last year to refer to the supreme court an important constitutional question relative to the respective rights of the provinces and of the Dominion with respect to power generated in connection with developments by the Dominion for navigation purposes. The hon. member has taken too little account of the answers which have been given by the supreme court to this question. They concern the relative rights of the Dominion and the provinces in relation to proprietary interest in and legislative control over waters with respect to navigation and water-powers made available by or in connection with works for the improvement of navigation.
Take the first recommendation of the resolution.-that a treaty be entered into immediately with the United States for the development and generation of water-power on the St. Lawrence river. My hon. friend's remarks directed to the government with respect to water-powers have for the most part been to the effect that this government has no right whatever to deal with the question of water-powers; yet be now suggests, in the first clause of his resolution, that we should enter into a treaty with the United States in connection with the generation of water-power. Were the government to undertake to follow the hon. gentleman, I fancy we would not be able to proceed very far before he himself would be the first to object that we were exceeding our jurisdiction in entering a field of operation which is one with which the provinces are more particularly concerned.
I do not intend to review the various proposals of my hon. friend's resolution but rather to discuss the broad subject of the development of the St. Lawrence, because I take it that this is the theme which it was intended should be discussed upon the introduction of the resolution.
For over one hundred years past the St. Lawrence river has afforded a common highway and transportation outlet to the peoples in the interior of this continent, whether residing in Canada or in the United States. In that period of time the St. Lawrence highway has been the subject of many treaties and conventions and its development has been, as well, a matter of continuous effort and consideration. I have in my hand a report of a special committee of the senate of Canada which was appointed at the last session, to inquire into the development and improvement of the St. Lawrence river. At page 7 of that report there ds a chapter entitled, "A Quarter of a Century of International Negotiation". This chapter, which was prepared by Mr. Yates, the Assistant Deputy Minister of the Department of Railways and Canals, sets out the more important stages in the negotiations between Canada and the United States respecting the St. Lawrence river development. In discussing this matter I intend to use the word "negotiations" in the same sense in which it is used in this report of the senate committee. Possibly the words "joint consideration" would be even more appropriate than the word "negotiation", lest by use of the latter term it might be inferred that steps have been taken which are of a binding character with respect to the particular project which is the subject of discussion at the present moment.
Reviewing negotiations which have taken place, it will be found that the most important step was taken twenty years ago when a treaty was entered into with respect to boundary waters. The treaty was made in 1909, and pursuant thereto the International Joint Commission was appointed, to which commission were referred, among other subjects, matters pertaining to the development of the St. Lawrence waterway. In 1919 the International Joint Commission took up more particularly the investigation of the feasibility of improving navigation facilities on the St. Lawrence between Montreal and lake Ontario so as to transform that section into an ocean shipway; its report was made to the governments of the United States and of Canada respectively in December, 1921. In that report the International Joint Commission strongly recommended the undertaking of the deepening of the St. Lawrence as an ocean shipway between Montreal and lake Ontario. The commission, however, advised that before a final decision was made there should be a further examination by a board of engineers with regard to engineering considerations, of which account would have to be taken. On
414	COMMONS
St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Mackenzie King
March 14, 1924, the president of the United States appointed what was known as the St. Lawrence River Commission, of which the Honourable Mr. Hoover, then Secretary of Commerce, now the president-elect of the United States, was made chairman. This commission was asked to consider the whole project in its economic and national aspects and to express an opinion as to whether the project should be undertaken. Shortly after the appointment of this commission by the United States government the government of Canada on May 7 appointed a body with similar functions. It is known [DOT]as the National Advisory Committee. Of that committee Right Hon. George P. Graham, the then Minister of Railways and Canals, was appointed chairman. By an exchange of notes between the two governments, through the arrangements brought about by these two bodies, a joint engineering board was a'p,pointed and instructed to review and extend the engineering plans as recommended by the International Joint Commission in 1921. The joint engineering board, composed of three representatives from the United States and three from Canada, went into matters very carefully and it made an elaborate re-survey of lake and river systems both as to navigation and power, and its report to both governments upon all the engineering aspects was presented on November 16, 1926. For the most part the report is unanimous; it is unanimous in its statement as to the feasibility and advisability of the improvement of the St. Lawrence waterway for navigation and power purposes. With reference to the advisability of the undertaking, if I am not mistaken, it draws attention to the fact that there are considerations of which each of the countries may wish to take account, but as an engineering project it makes it quite clear that the deepening of the St. Lawrence as a ship-way is wholly feasible. There was a difference of opinion between the engineers appointed by the United States government and those appointed by the Canadian government with respect to the best form of development; the United States engineers favoured a single stage development in the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river, while the Canadian engineers favoured a two-stage development in that section. This report was submitted to the United States St. Lawrence River Commission whose members accepted it and advised the United States government to do likewise. The commission recommended 
that negotiations should be entered into with the government of Canada in an endeavour to arrive at an agreement as to the development of the waterway. The government of the United States adopted the recommendations of the St. Lawrence River Commission and so advised the Canadian government. In this manner correspondence was opened between Canada and the United States in a series of communications which extended over the period April, 1927, to April, 1928.
The first communrioation was from the United States and was dated April 13, 1927. It proposed as I have already indicated that negotiations should be entered into to arrive at an agreement with respect to the deepening of the St. Lawrence as an ocean shipway, and Canada was invited to become a part}'' to such an agreement. At the time this communication was received the advisory board in Canada was awaiting appendices to the report of the joint board of engineers which contained alternative plans with respect to the development of the international rapids section, and the board advised the government not to reply finally to the request with respect to an agreement until they had been given an opportunity to consider in its entirety the report of the joint board of engineers. Accordingly on July 12 a communication was sent to the United States government advising that there would be a delay in answering its request but that when we had received further information from our national advisory board we would reply, discussing the whole situation, including the proposal made.
In January, 1928. the national advisory committee made its report to the Dominion government. The committee had received a full report from the joint engineering board, and in its report to the government it set out what in its opinion was the nature of the reply which should be made by Canada to the United States. Subsequently a reply was sent to the United States government very much along the lines indicated by the national advisory committee. That reply pointed out that in addition to the engineering features there were important financial and economic considerations which Canada would require to be taken into account and also that, with regard to one particular phase of the matter, namely, the export of power, it would have to be distinctly understood we could not consider any agreement which would involve the exportation of power from Canada to the United States.

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Mackenzie King
Perhaps in passing I might touch on this point specifically. It is the last one referred to in the resolution of my hon. friend and is one which it might be well to have in mind in connection with any further consideration of the matter. Our government has repeatedly made clear its policy with respect to the exportation of power from Canada to the United States. We have given it as our opinion that power should not be exported. That opinion was endorsed by the national advisory committee with respect to the power which might be generated in connection with the development of the St. Lawrence. Accordingly, in writing the United States with respect to any possible basis of negotiation, our position in this regard was made very clear. The exact statement made by our government will be found in the correspondence which passed between the United States and Canada all of which was tabled in this house on April 17, of last year. In that correspondence will be found a communication dated January 31, 1928, which contains these words:
Reference was made in your note to the early development of hydro-electric power as a factor which must have equal application to and influence upon the Dominion of Canada. The opportunity of developing great quantities of power incidental to navigation is, it is agreed, a special advantage possesed by the St. Lawrence project, and an important consideration in determining its advisability. In this aspect of the project, however, there are again special features in the Canadian situation which it is desirable to make clear. Public opinion in Canada is opposed to the export of hydroelectric power, and is insistent that such power as may he rendered available on the St. Lawrence, whether from the wholly Canadian section, or from the Canadian half of the international section, shall be utilized within the Dominion to stimulate Canadian industry and d avelop the natural resources. With this view the national advisory committee expresses itself as in complete accord.
When the United States government replied to our communication it was made perfectly clear that from the point of view of the United States, Canada was entirely within her rights in taking such a position, and that no question would be raised on the part of the United States with respect tbeireto. This recognition of Canada's attitude and right will be found in the communication dated March 12, 1928. and is as follows:
The United States fully recognizes the right of the Dominion of Canada to the ownership and use of the Canadian share of the power which may be developed in the international section of the waterway as well as to all that developed in the national section and it recognizes also that the disposition of the power is purely a domestic question. It recognizes further that this share is an inherent attribute of Canadian sovereignty, irrespective of the agency by which the power may be developed.

speechtext:
I have not
here the phraseology used, but I have been corresponding with the Premier of Ontario with respect to the matter, and I have had in mind the rapids section referred to by the joint engineers in their report, and I am sure Mr. Ferguson had the same waters in mind. These waters are part of the international section of the St. Lawrence.
In its communication to the United States government replying to the possibility of our entering into negotiations to arrive, at a treaty with respect to the deepening of the St. Lawrence, the Canadian government sought to bring to the attention of the United States government all considerations which were likely to be material factors in arriving at any settlement. These questions were brought up at the outset so that there might be no doubt in the minds of either the Canadian public or the American public as to the basis on which we would be prepared to proceed with negotiations, which basis we regarded as allimportant. In this regard mention was made first, of certain financial considerations; secondly, of certain economic considerations; thirdly, of the engineering considerations; and fourthly, a matter to which I have not as yet referred, of the constitutional question between the provinces and the Dominion as to their relative rights in the matter of water powers made available by or in connection with works for the improvement of navigation.
May I pause for a moment to say a word as to the constitutional question. In the fall of 1927 a Dominion-provincial conference was held in this city, at which questions of concern to the provinces and ourselves were freely discussed. At that conference the premiers of Ontario and Quebec brought up the question of power rights as between the Dominion and the provinces where the power was generated as a result of developments for navigation purposes. We were asked if we would refer

that subject to the Supreme Court to get an opinion as to the respective rights of the provinces and the Dominion. We agreed to do so, and on January 18, 1928, the Dominion government presented a series of questions to the Supreme Court with respect to the relative rights, interests, powers and control of the Dominion and the provinces respectively as they pertained to power and navigation. After these questions had been submitted we were asked by the provinces if we would agree to supplement them by other questions which would clarify the position as to the rights of the provinces with respect to power. Complying with that request, the original order in council of January 18 was amended on April 14 to include two additional questions which the provinces wished to have added to .the original questions submitted. The Supreme Court had its hearing on these matters in October, and within the month past has given its answers to the questions which were submitted.

I will come to that in a few minutes.
The conference between the provinces and the Dominion having taken place in the month of November and before our reply was sent to the United States, we felt that we should draw the attention of the United States to the fact that these constitutional questions had been raised by the provinces at this conference, and the fact that we were submitting to the Supreme Court, a series of questions, and asking the Supreme Court for answers thereto. What we asked the United States in so many words was whether the United States would be prepared, when it came to negotiating, to accept as a basis of negotiation what, we had indicated] we would wish to have taken into account with respect to finances; what we had indicated would have to be taken into account with respect to economic conditions; what might have to be taken into account as the result of the answers made by the supreme court to the questions which had been submitted. Finally, we made mention of the Dominion's desire to have a conference with the provinces immediately concerned, namely, Ontario and Quebec, before giving a final answer to the United States in reference to the suggested agreement. In other words,

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Mackenzie King
our .communication sent on January 31, 1928, outlined the considerations of which we felt Canada would have to take account, and asked if the procedure outlined would afford " an acceptable 'basis of negotiation," in which event we would then consult with the provinces, once the supreme court's answers to our questions were given.
The reply, dated March 12, which we received from the United States, was with respect to all these matters broadly in the affirmative. The government of the United States said that While it could not say that lit agreed with all that was set out in the report of the advisory committee, nevertheless it felt inclined to regard as an acceptable basis of negotiation a proposal along the general lines indicated, namely, along what had been suggested with respect to a division of costs, what had been referred to as economic considerations of which we would have to take account, and the matter of there being no exportation of hydro-electric power as the result of any agreement that might be entered into, and finally, the understanding that the Dominion should, before seeking any final settlement, have a conference with the provinces immediately concerned. I think that covers fainly accurately most of the essential points. It was suggested that the two countries should proceed with the appointment of commissioners to discuss jointly the problems presented with a view to the formulation of a convention. We replied on April 5. 1928, that Canada recognized that an acceptable basis of negotiation had been found sufficiently definite to enable us to take the next step, namely, that of consultation with the provinces concerned, following which we would be in a position to make an appropriate reply to the United States. The United States on April 7 agreed that our government should take up this matter with the provinces.
With regard to the engineering features the United States government also intimated that it could see no objection to the Dominion engineers conferring with the engineers of the province of Ontario with a view of seeing whether an agreement might not be reached between Ontario and the Dominion as to the best plan of development of the international rapids section. The United States went a step further and indicated that after the province and the Dominion had come to an agreement on engineering features with respect to the Canadian point of view, they would be quite willing to refer the whole engineering aspect of the question back of the joint board of engineers with a view to seeing whether there could not be, as there 7S594-27
would necessarily have to be in time, unanimity with respect to the plan of development of the international rapids section.
I	hope I have made clear what the difference really is with respect to the development of the international section. The United States engineers preferred a one-stage development; they preferred that because they believed it would be less costly; that more power could be developed at a less cost, and that it would obviate the necessity of the construction of one lock. The Canadian engineers preferred a two-stage development, believing that it would avoid the necessity of constructing the large embankments or levees necessitated by the single-stage plan, which the Canadian engineers thought would be viewed with some concern by communities in the immediate vicinity. It was also felt by the Canadian engineers that a two-stage development would permit of the power being developed and marketed by degrees; that the power from the first stage would be available before the second stage was commenced, and that by the time the second stage was completed, the country would be in a position to absorb the further power.
