The United States government suggested in the communication to which I have just referred, that it might be unnecessary to wait until the engineers had completed their further consideration of the projects, before appointing commissioners to draft the convention that might serve as a means of bringing about an agreement. It was suggested that possibly commissioners might be appointed and the work of arranging an agreement proceeded with while the engineers were doing their technical work; that they would be called upon to advise any commission that might be appointed and that the two could proceed concurrently. At this point in April of last year the correspondence between the Dominion and the United States concluded.
From April up to the present time there has been no further correspondence for the reason that we have been awaiting the answers by the supreme court to the questions which were submitted to it. The answers were given at the beginning of this month. Hon. members must already be familiar, if not with the text, at least with the general nature of them. We had hoped we might find in the answers which

41S	COMMONS
St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Mackenzie King
the supreme court would give to the questions submitted to it, a solution to the very intricate and involved question of the relative rights of the provinces and the Dominion with respect to power. But while the answers which have been given by the supreme court have clarified certain points, they certainly do not help very much in making clear many of the questions that are of importance with respect to the relative rights of the provinces and the Dominion in the matter of power. The court did not find itself able to give a very definite answer to several of the more important questions submitted. It will apparently be difficult to secure from the courts by submission of questions of general scope any definite or precise finding. In so many words, the judges of the supreme court say-and their opinion is unanimous-that it is impossible, from a series of abstract questions, to give concrete answers which will meet all situations which may arise; that the only way in which, so far as the courts are concerned, definite answers may be expected with regard to this involved question, is to have each case submitted and decided on its merits.
This much is clear, and here I come to answer my hon. friend who interrupted me a moment ago. From the opinion of the supreme court it would seem that we might wait from now to the day of judgment, if I may use that expression, to get from any court an opinion conclusive enough to settle as between the Dominion and the provinces all of the questions with respect to their relative rights in the matter of power. So far as we can be guided by the opinion of the supreme court, it would appear that if an appeal from the answers which they have given were taken to the privy council, we could expect nothing more from the privy council in the way of definiteness than what we have already obtained from the supreme court. In the circumstances, having sought in the first instance a solution of the constitutional question by an appeal to the courts, and having received the replies which we have received, the government is of opinion that it is in the interests of all concerned, of the provinces and of the Dominion in their relations to each other, as well as of the Dominion in its relation to the United States in dealing with this question of international waterways, that we should not seek for the present at least to settle this matter by any further reference to the courts, but that we should endeavour to seek a solution by direct conference between the provinces immediately concerned and ourselves. Accordingly the government has decided, as we advised the United States government we would decide when we received the replies

from the supreme court, to ask the governments of Ontario and Quebec to meet us in conference, to see if it is not possible to arrive by agreement between us at some settlement which will secure the provinces in their full rights with respect to power, and secure the Dominion with respect to all national interests involved. We are at the present time sending communications to the Premier of Ontario and to the Premier of Quebec asking that, as soon after this session of parliament is over as may be convenient to them, they meet us in conference, that we may see as a result of direct conference whether it is not possible for us to come to an agreement which, as I have said, will permit without further question the development of the power in which the provinces are interested, and which will secure the Dominion in all its rights in respect to navigation and power, and which will enable the St. Lawrence development to go forward on such lines as may be agreed upon between the provinces and ourselves; in other words, to see if it is not possible to work out a plan of St. Lawrence development which will safeguard any interests of the provinces in the development of power as well as the national interests.
That is the present position, and I submit that it would not have been (possible for the government 'to have proceeded in this matter more rapidly or more effectively in any other way than by the method I have described. Had we met the provinces without referring the constitutional question in the first instance to the supreme court, we would have been in the dark as to what in the event of a submission we might expect. We know now the point at which we are likely to arrive as the result of submission to the court of questions with respect to constitutional rights in the matter of power. But we see no reason why, speaking for the federal government, it should not now be possible for the Premier of Ontario and the Premier of Quebec, with a group of their colleagues, to meet with members of the federal government and, actuated by a desire to remove those differences and uncertainties which make for friction and create doubt as between the provinces and the Dominion, to work out some sort of settlement which will be satisfactory to all concerned. In other words, we are following in regard to Ontario and Quebec the method which we have followed in our dealings with the other provinces of Canada. We have attempted, for instance, to deal with the problems which were uppermost in the minds of our friends in the maritimes by going carefully by direct negotiation into the questions which are of greatest concern to them. We

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Mackenzie King
are taking up by direct negotiation with members of the western governments the questions of the transfer of the natural resources which are the outstanding and immediate questions so far as they are concerned. So1 far as the two old provinces of Ontario and Quebec are concerned the question of power development, and the question of the development of the St. Lawrence channel as an ocean shipway, are the matters which are of prime importance, and it as our hope, indeed, it is our expectation, that meeting together with a sincere desire to work out a solution of these problems, we shall be able to find a satisfactory solution.
I	say that with the more confidence because of experiences that we have already had. I referred a moment ago to the dominion-provincial conference held in 1927, at which conference there were a number of very intricate problems. With respect to many of those problems we were able by conference to find a solution to the satisfaction of the governments concerned. With respect to this very matter of power and navigation rights, we were able to make some progress in one important particular. Since the conference was held there has been an agreement with the province of Ontario with regard to the preservation of the scenic beauty of Niagara falls. That agreement involved, in a small way to be sure, but, nevertheless, involved practically all the considerations that are likely to come up in, this larger issue. We were dealing there with international waterways; we were dealing there with power rights; we were dealing there as well with questions that had to be made the subject of agreement with our neighbours across the line, questions which in the long run could be dealt with only by treaty; but we were able by our engineers working in conjunction with the hydro-electric engineers, through goodwill, to find a solution w-hich was satisfactory to Ontario, satisfactory to the Dominion, and satisfactory to the United States, and a solution which I believe will be found satisfactory to this House of Commons when the treaty will be submitted! for approval, as I hope it may be to-morrow.
But there is another reason why we feel encouraged in regard to the matter, and it is this:	Some time ago we drew the attention
of the Premier of Ontario to the fact that the hydro-electric engineers had prepared plans with respect to a two-stage development of the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence different from those of the Dominion engineers, and that as we were 78594-27*
negotiating or expecting to negotiate with the United States in regard to the St. Lawrence Waterway development, we felt if any headway were to be made in this -matter it was important that there should be complete cooperation between the provincial government of Ontario and the Dominion government. I am happy to say that as recently as Saturday last I received from Premier Ferguson a communication in which Mr. Ferguson expresses regret, for reasons which from his letter are obvious, at not having been able to reply sooner to the communication which had been sent to him, and saying that he would be pleased to appoint two engineers, and naming on behalf of the Ontario government two engineers, to meet with the engineers of the Dominion government. This is a first essential step in, settling this phase of the matter as between the Dominion and the province of Ontario. So I say that, to say the least, the signs are propitious.
In addition to that, other matters have progressed which up to the present time have tended somewhat to complicate the situation. One of the most troublesome questions with which the Canadian government was confronted each time a discussion took place on the St. Lawrence waterway was the diversion at Chicago of large quantities of water from the great lakes through the Chicago Sanitary District canal. Well, this much can be said with regard to the Chicago diversion, that more progress has been made in the last four or five years towards getting that matter satisfactorily settled than had been made in all the previous period of the diversion. The Secretary of State for War of the United States, in giving his permit to the Chicago Sanitary District in 1925 to divert a certain quantity of water, did so on the condition that that diversion must gradually be lessened. It provided for a steady reduction of the diversion and for the construction of sewage works and for metering the domestic supply as means of reducing the volume of water withdrawn. The joint board of engineers have definitely ascertained and set forth the effect of the diversion on the levels of the great lakes. That point is now beyond controversy. As a result of the verdict of the United States Supreme Court recently given in the case of the Lake States versus The State of Illinois it has been made clear that the diversion for sewerage purposes does not rest on any legal basis, and it is provided that the Hon. Charles Evans Hughes, as master, is to report on a procedure to be followed which, while according the sanitary district a reasonably practicable time to pro-
420	COMMONS
St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Mackenzie King
vide other means of disposing of the sewage, will ensure the speedy and continuous reduction of the diversion. Therefore with respect to the Chicago diversion and to the position at Niagara, within the recent past, the situation has materially bettered.
As indicated, we have been seeking to cooperate with Ontario in its power problems, and we have been doing the same with respect to Quebec. The province of Quebec, like the province of Ontario, is interested in power development. The province has certain rights with respect to power developments; we have certain rights with respect to the protection of navigation. In any negotiations with the province of Quebec, and with respect to the approval of any plans which may be submitted by any company holding a charter from that province, we shall take and are taking great care to see that nothing shall be granted to a company or to the province which in any way wild impede or interfere with the St. Lawrence development project, or the full rights of the Dominion in navigation on the St. Lawrence. Viewing the matter broadly, therefore, it would appear as though it required only the good will of all parties interested to work out some agreement as between the provinces and the Dominion which would settle this vexed constitutional problem in a manner satisfactory to all .concerned, and which in addition would enable the provinces and ourselves to take a course which in their interest and the interest of Canada as a whole would be considered most advantageous in negotiating with the United States with respect to further development of the St. Lawrence shipway.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I say a word or two with reference to the security of this Dominion in any negotiations with the United States relative to the deepening of the St. Lawrence. Mr. Ferguson, in answer to one or two questions which have been put to him recently, has made a very obvious reply, namely, that for his part he will not, in dealings with the United States, countenance anything which will affect the sovereign rights of Canada, that he will not in the slightest particular part with any sovereign right which the Dominion has, nor will he permit that right to be threatened or impaired in the least. That sentiment will, I believe, be echoed by every individual in this Dominion -certainly in this parliament. I cannot think of an hon. member who would for one moment contemplate any kind of an agreement with the United States which would impair in the least the sovereignty of this country with respect to any rights which it now has. And may I say further, I do not believe the

United States would think of negotiating with Canada on a basis which involved or contemplated anything of that character. However, let me make it perfectly clear that with respect to the St. Lawrence development, whatever steps are taken hon. members may rest assured, and the country may rest assured, that in no particular will any of the severeign rights of this Dominion with respect to power or navigation be impaired in the least, or even be made subject to the possibility of impairment.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: Does the right hon. gentleman say the same with respect to the rights of the provinces?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
I would certainly say the same with respect to the rights of the provinces. There is a good deal of what I think might be termed loose talking with respect to some phases of the St. Lawrence development. Why it is indulged in, I am at a loss to understand. I think we would be wise to get at the truth and stick to the truth in public discussion and in the discussion of international questions above all others. For example we hear it sometimes said that under no circumstances should there be permitted an international waterway which will not be an all-Canadian waterway, that so far as the St. Lawrence and great lakes are concerned there must be an all Canadian water route and that on no account is there to be any going 'backwards and forwards as between the United States and Canada. Now, those who speak in that way cannot have the least knowledge-or if they have they are not applying it-as to what is existing at this moment and has existed for years past, and as to what the engineers who have appeared before committees of parliament, and in particular the committee of the Senate to which I have referred, have made very plain, namely, that at the present time the utilized channel through the great lakes and the St. Lawrence is not a channel which is all within the waters of Canada or all within the waters of the United States, but is a channel which part of the way is in American waters and part of the way in Canadian. That is the position now, and in all the development of the St. Lawrence and the Great lakes that has thus far taken place, that fact has been recognized. The United States has taken care of some parts of the channel, Canada has taken care of other parts. Both countries, according to the treaty signed in 1909, have equal navigation rights in the Great lakes and the international section of the St. Lawrence. So when there

St. Laurence Waterway-Mr. Mackenzie King
is a discussion about having an all-Canadian route, let us understand exactly what that means. It does not mean, the construction today of some small portion of a water route in one province or in another, but it means changing existing routes to an extent that, engineers tell us, will involve-I do not know the figures, but the expenditure will run into many millions of dollars.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: Hundreds of millions of dollars.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
That proposal can only be put forward for the purpose in some way or another of confusing the public mind with respect to this great and important project.
In conclusion let me say a further word as to the security of this country in all negotiations with our neighbour to the south, with respect to international waterways or any other negotiations that may need consideration. The St. Lawrence waterway and the great lakes are in considerable part international waters. A broad division can be made. There is a portion of the St. Lawrence which is wholly within Canada, there remains the balance of the St. Lawrence which is in the nature of an international waterway as are the great lakes up to Sault Ste. Marie and beyond. With respect, to the international section, the nation's rights are already secured by treaty, and those treaty rights, both as regards Canada and the United States, are supreme over anything that can be done by the government of either country. The treaty lays down very clearly that any works materially affecting the level of these boundary waters must be approved either (by special agreement between Canada and the United States or by the International Joint Commission. That is under the boundary water treaty of 1909, and it applies to what may be done by the governor in council or what may be done by act of parliament; because a treaty overrides both and is supreme.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: But there is a treaty, prior to that in point of time, on which our rights are .based. So I apprehend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
As I have said, there is a series of treaties; I made that clear at the outset. As regards my hon. friend's remark, I repeat: Every right secured by any treaty will be maintained in any negotiations. Treaty rights are supreme in every respect. But what I am seeking to make clear at the moment is this. The sense of security which this parliament has a right to feel with respect to whatever may be done on the St. Lawrence, whether in the international section or in the national-and I am dealing for the moment with the international-is wholly ample. Our rights in the international section are secured by treaty.
Let us come to the national section. And may I pause here to say a word as to the bill which was introduced by the same hon. member who has moved this resolution- the bill providing for some enlargement of the Navigable Waters Protection Act. It is very seldom that on a question of this kind particularly where there has been much in the way of general discussion, the hon. member when he concludes is not followed by some other hon. gentleman in the house. The government had expected, seeing that the subject with which his bill dealt was one that had been considerably discussed in the public prints and elsewhere, that a good deal would be said by hon. members opposite with respect to various phases of the matter.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: Why not on the government side?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
The government intended to make its position quite clear. But I confess that we were taken very much by surprise when no one followed the hon. gentleman, and therefore no reply was made immediately. A complete reply could have been made in ten minutes and would have avoided the division we bad on that occasion. That reply would have been in effect very much the statement which I am now making. Apart from the fact-and I do not think mv hon. friend relished it either-that in voting for the hon. member's bill he was endorsing retroactive legislation, which I do not believe he likes, every hon. member who supported that bill was endorsing legislation which was unwise in other respects. They were voting in support of a measure which was in no sense necessary to attain the object at which it was assumed to be aimed, and which had it carried would have rendered many necessary developments impossible.
As I have said, in regard to the international section of the St. Lawrence, parliament's security is obtained through the treaty. With regard to the national section, assuming that as a result of anything done in that section the waters which are a part of the international section are raised, such action becomes the subject of review on the part of the International Joint Commission in precisely the same way as if the particular action were being taken in the international section.
Further with respect to the portion of the St. Lawrence which is wholly within Canada, and indeed in respect to all navigable waters, this
422	COMMONS
St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Mackenzie King
parliament is already secured in its powers of supervision under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, which gives to (parliament the right not merely to review (but to annul whatever may 'be done by the governor in council should it be shown that in any particular the action taken is unwise. Let me give to the house the sections of the Navigable Waters Protection Act- bearing upon this question. Section 4 reads:
No work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless tbe site thereof has been approved by the governor in council, nor unless such work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with plans and regulations approved or made by the governor in council.
Section 10 provides:
The governor in council may make such orders or regulations as he deems expedient for navigation purposes respecting any work to which _ this part applies or of which the plan and site are approved under any act of the parliament of Canada.
2. The local authority, company or person constructing, owning or in possession of any work shall be subject to such orders or regulations.
I come now to section 12, which is the important provision. This is the section which I wish hon. members to note particularly:
Parliament may, at any time, annul or vary any order of the governor in council made under this part.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: Parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
Yes, parliament. Subsection 2 goes on:
Any action of parliament in that behalf shall not he deemed an infringement of the rights of the local authority, company or person concerned.
Where then is the need for adding anything further to this particular act? My hon. friend the member for North Winnipeg (Mr, Heaps) asked me the other day as to whether parliament would have the right to review certain matters which might be in contemplation. He has no need for concern as to the powers of parliament with respect to the possible acts of the government he had in mind whether they were of to-day or of six months ago or are still of the future; because parliament, with respect to the protection of navigable matters under the act as it stands, has the power not only to review but to annul whatever may be done by the governor in council. Words cannot be stronger.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman realizes that he is opening up debate on a question already disposed of by the house., and this may involve the house in a rather protracted discussion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
I am merely
seeking to make plain the points that bear particularly upon the St. Lawrence water development. I am not dealing with the other question; to that I have referred only incidentally. But this is very material to the question of the St. Lawrence development with respect to the rights of this parliament touching any act of the government, by order in council or otherwise.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: Would it not be better sometimes not to pass an order in council than to have to annul it afterwards?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
My hon. friend has asked a reasonable question, and I am glad that he has done so. There are some matters which are administrative in character and others which are legislative; there are some questions which are technical and which can be dealt with only by experts, and other questions which are suitable for discussion in a deliberative assembly. When one comes to such questions as sites for water-power, the volume or rapidity of water passing over a particular point, the question of the effect of obstructions upon the levels of waters, the effect of the ice flow in certain localities, all of which are important questions when we are dealing with navigation, these questions can be settled and settled only by expert engineers; they cannot be settled in a deliberative assembly. Most questions that relate to public works are of that character; they are questions for the experts bf the government departments; and parliament in its wisdom has made clear that it is not advisable to prevent development by requiring in the first instance that .parliament itself shall perform functions or duties which it is not at all fitted to perform. That is the reason this section is worded in the way it is. In other words, so far as provincial rights may be concerned, what is sought by the Navigable Waters Protection Act is to allow, the full development which provinces may seek with respect to power but where navigation is likely to be affected to assure at the same time that the general interest will be wholly and adequately secured.
May I add just one word. The section which I have read makes it quite clear that parliament has the power at any time to annul any act of the government which may be contrary to the public interest where wc are dealing with works which may affect navigable waters, but in regard to negotiations such as those affecting the St. Lawrence development parliament has a further security. Under our general policy we have laid it down that before a treaty is finally ratified it shall

SI. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Bennett
be. brought to this parliament for approval, and I wish to repeat now the assurance given parliament not once but on different occasions that if at any time, while this administration is in office, a treaty is arrived at between the United States and Canada with respect to the development of the St. Lawrence waterway, that treaty will be brought to thi3 parliament and not ratified until parliament has approved of it.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
Why could not the same
principle apply to any scheme entered into with regard to the development of the St. Lawrence river?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: I have already distinguished between that part of the St Lawrence which is in the international section and the part which is in the national section. Panliament's ultimate control of both sections is secured under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, while additional security with respect to the international section is afforded by bringing a treaty to parliament for its approval.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
I am speaking only of the
principle of having parliament ratify something before it is ratified by the cabinet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
There again,
as I tried to explain to my hon. friend from Bow River, there are technical features which can be worked out only by engineers. In negotiating an agreement with respect to water-power, water rights and navigation, where the considerations are so largely technical in their nature, parliament is scarcely in a position to discuss such matters in detail; it is for experts to work out these matters.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
But I am
afraid my right hon. friend is on the horns of a dilemma in this case. If because of a lack of technical knowledge parliament is incapable of arriving at an intelligent decision in the first place, lacking that technical knowledge how is parliament to arrive at an intelligent decision with regard to the annulment of an order in council later?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
As my hon.
friend knows, you can present a final plan to parliament, you can have a committee before which you can bring your experts fhlly to explain a matter, but you do not begin a project of development in that way. You could not construct a street railway in that manner. You must have your plans and your agreement practically consummated before they can be properly discussed in an assembly such as this.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
But the
right hon. gentleman is aware that that is how we have worked in several cases.. For example, when we considered the question of harnessing the tides of the bay of Fundy, we had a committee go into the whole matter and consider all the details. Why not do the same in this case?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: I do not think those tides have been harnessed yet.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
No, but
we have passed upon the plans.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
I do not think any plans or details were submitted. However, I wish to make clear the government's point of view, that so far as the St. Lawrence project is concerned, whether it refers to our relations with the provinces or our relations with the United States, this government intends to see that the rights of Canada are fully protected.
Having said that much, Mr. Speaker, may I conclude by reminding the house that in some respects the present moment is perhaps a critical one at which to discuss an international matter which affects our relations with our neighbours to the south. I do not wish to discourage discussion in any way; in fact I welcome all that may be said, but in debating this matter I hope hon. gentlemen will bear in mind the fact that whatever is said in this parliament at this time may have a very far-reaching effect upon some decisions which may be reached in the veiy near future with regard to matters which are of real concern to both countries. With that one word, which I think it well to say at this time, I will conclude my remarks.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: What is critical in the situation with regard to the United States at this time?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I only wish to
observe that it is somewhat strange that a matter of such transcendent importance to the people of Canada should be now discussed by the Prime Minister on the resolution of a private member. The policy of the administration with respect to a matter of such far-reaching importance should have been stated on an occasion when there w'ould be ample opportunity for debate altogether apart from the resolution moved by a private member which only expresses his opinion with respect to the subject matter of the discussion
We advised the government last year not only in this but in a similar matter as well that any reference to the Supreme Court of
424	COMMONS
St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Bennett
Canada with respect to any matter in the form of questions amounted to nothing more than obtaining the opinion of the law officers of the crown. The Privy Council has so stated, and in a judgment of Right Hon. Mr. Justice Duff, speaking for the Supreme Court, be indicated that their decision was based on that view. It must be remembered also, as Lord Loreburn observed, that the legislative always controls the executive branch of government, and I take it that the right hon. gentleman, in seeking a reason for the attitude of the house the other evening, will find it in that sentence, "The legislative always controls the executive branch of government." This' house has lost confidence in the way its executive has dealt with the water powers of the St. Lawrence river. We know from the public press, from the discussions of gentlemen who support the government and from the different opinions expressed privately, not to me but to others, by members of the government itself, that this house has good reason to express its loss of confidence in the way the government, as a government, is dealing with the problems connected with the St. Lawrence waterways. That is the real reason why this house voted the other evening as it did, because the members realized that iD the exercise of that second branch of the executive s power, namely the legislative branch, they were exercising that power in a manner inimicable to the public interest of Canada, or at least in a manner that threatened to be so.
When the right hon. Prime Minister refers to the question of retroactive legislation he realizes that it was retroactive to the first day of this year, 1929, a not unusual thing with respect to legislation similar in character to that particular legislation, because it was felt that if matters of such transcendent importance as the utilization of the St. Lawrence river for a ship-way, with the incidental development of power, were to be considered as they should be considered, then it would be better to present them for the approval of parliament rather than have the government commit this country to a certain line of action and then later say we may annul it. I wonder which is the worse retroactive legislation, which would permit a private company after expending say $25,000,000, have its rights cancelled and the payment of damages demanded. Is that what the Prime Minister means when he refers to the Navigable Waters Protection Act and says there is power contained therein to annul an order in council after it has been enacted, after rights have been acquired under it, vast fMr. Bennett.]
expenditures made, and securities issued under it, held in every part of the world? Does he say then that this parliament can annul it? Could anything be more ridiculous than an observation of that character? Could anything be more in keeping with the idea that is at the basis of our institutions, namely, that nothing of that sort can be done unless compensation is paid?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
I think my
hon. friend knows the section of the act which
intimates that damages cannot be claimed.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
I am coming to that.
What the right hon. gentleman is endeavouring to do is to make it impossible for anyone to finance any undertaking based upon approval being given by this government, if it is covered by the Navigable Waters Protection Act. What will the life insurance companies, who are told these securities are trustee securities, say when they are told that this parliament has the right to annul under this act, the order in council under which an undertaking is commenced and render the securities valueless without compensation?

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: They have been doing it for years.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: Annulling them?

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: Selling the securities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: It has been the law for years.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
For the simple and
obvious reason that never in the history of our parliament has any such matter been submitted to parliament. It has been suggested by the Prime Minister that there is power under the act to destroy that which the executive has done. This involves consequences most far-reaching, but I am content to leave it at that for it is not a matter of importance at the moment. I will only say that the Prime Minister of Canada has suggested that when his executive gives approval with respect to any given undertaking that may interfere with navigation or otherwise, or where powers are called into operation, by reason of the provision of the Navigable Waters Protection Act this parliament may annul it and destroy it without compensation being paid the security holders.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
It is not my
suggestion, it is a statement of law.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
But it is suggested in
order that hon. gentlemen who have raised certain questions may ease their consciences by saying that this parliament can do something which this parliament has never been asked to do, and which I cannot think this

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Bennett
parliament would ever consider doing, for the simple and obvious reason that it is provided in the constitution that there can be no exercise of any such power. This country cannot now undo that which has been lawfully done. Daniel O'Connell once said, " Parliament is omnipotent." Parliament might have the power to annul an order in council, but the exercise of that power would absolutely destroy the credit of Canada.
I wonder if the right hon. gentleman recalls the difference between what was sought to be done in the power case and what was done by his illustrious predecessor? Certain railway interests made an agreement with Sir Wilfrid Laurier's government, whereby the government parted with the gold-bearing lands of the Yukon subject to the approval of parliament. The House of Commons gave approval to that agreement made by the then Minister of the Interior with the Mackenzie and Mann interests, but the senate threw it out. No man will say that that was not a proper exercise of power at that time, but the problem that confronts this house, to which the right hon. gentleman has referred, whereby this country can no longer safely continue to rely upon the sound exercise of its powers by the executive on its legislative side, is entirely different. It was only a few short years ago that this country resounded with cries uttered by the right hon. gentleman and those who sit beside him, about orders in council and government by orders in council. There was not one part of this country where the supporters of the right hon. gentleman did not go decrying orders in council. The Seven Sisters falls has been parted with by an order in council; there are the St. Lawrence orders in council; and an enormous part of the public domain in Alberta has been parted with for the purpose of grazing lands for a period of twenty-one years under orders in council. These grants were made in areas withdrawn from settlement, but if the government continues to part with these lands the western provinces will find themselves without public domain; the Dominion government will have parted with all the crown lands before they are transferred to the provinces. That is the position.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
Will the
hon. gentleman name any sections of Alberta that have been granted by lease and that were not formerly under lease?

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
I refer to those areas
that had lapsed, south of Medicine Hat, in which a gentleman from Windsor has been very active and about which I trust this house will be fully informed at a later date.
Section 12 of chapter 140 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, reads as follows:
Parliament may, at any time, annul or vary any order of the governor in council made under this part.
That is, under the regulations.

speechtext: No, no.

speechtext:

speechtext: Part 1 and part 2 are distinctly set out; one deals with public works and the other with marine and fisheries.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: The section says, " shall not be deemed an infringement of the rights of the local authority, company or person concerned." subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: My hon. friend is arguing for the other side.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: I am presenting both sides, certainly. I will say very frankly to the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) that I do not believe the Dominion of Canada ever placed upon the statute books a statute which would enable public works to be destroyed without compensation and thus ruin the credit of Canada. The hon. gentleman has surely followed what was said. I said that if the suggestion made by the right hon. the Prime Minister is sound, and in which the Solicitor General concurred, that this parliament could annul an order in council granting approval to the erection of works in the St. Lawrence, it would destroy the securities if no compensation were paid. I am content to leave it at that. I say that parliament never intended to have placed upon the act the construction which has been placed upon it by the Solicitor General and the Prime Minister.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext: What about the other argument?

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
I say the other argument is a sound argument; parliament never in-
426	COMMONS

tended to destroy rights created under an authorization that had been given and before such authorization had been annulled.

I was presenting the fallacy of its being suggested that this parliament should nullify the consent given by the executive, and I was content with that. However, at the moment I will adopt the language of Mr. Gladstone, which was that he would not prescribe until he was called in. I can only say that if the right hon. gentleman continues the course that has been indicated this afternoon, it will not be long before we are called in.
The question the right hon. gentleman has discussed this afternoon is a question of profound importance to the Canadian people. It is correct to say that for more than a quarter of a century it has engaged their attention. It is also important to point out that under the treaty of 1909, upon which such stress was laid, we have the old story of an even numbered tribunal, and all the consequent results that follow from that. I think the right hon. gentleman is right in saying that it is not desirable at this time to discusss this matter at length. I quite agree with him that there are reasons why it might well be discussed on some other occasion, and that is the reason why I had hoped that, rather than on the motion of a private member, the government itself would declare its policy as it has done this afternoon.
The rights with respect to the international section of the St. Lawrence river are determined by a treaty entered into between Her Majesty, Queen Victoria, and the United States of America. Those words we may modify and we may affect by a new treaty. At the moment that new treaty has not been negotiated. The right hon. gentleman in his correspondence has indicated to the United States that we are prepared to enter into a discussion and to negotiate a treaty dealing with power rights and navigation rights on the St. Lawrence river.

speechtext: What I have said is wholly consistent with what the right hon. gentleman observes, except that he has overlooked this, namely, that we stated that we were prepared to enter into discussions with respect to the matter with the United States of America, but that pending the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, those discussions could not be carried forward. That is the sense of the note which the right hon. gentleman sent to the United States, he made it quite clear-and it is a matter which should be made quite clear-that until there was a final determination either by negotiation and ratification or by judicial interpretation of the rights between the provinces and the Dominion, the Dominion would not enter into a treaty that might thereafter be found, in a concrete case, to use the language of the judgment of the court, to be wholly beyond the jurisdiction of the Dominion. That is the position -which the right hon. gentleman's note indicated the executive took. That is a position from which this afternoon he has not departed, but to which he has added this, that now the. judgment of the supreme court has been delivered, which judgment indicates that the questions are incapable of being answered, and that, if answered, are no better than the opinion of the law officers of the crown the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) being one of them, those answers are no more important than opinions of the Attorney General and Solicitor General of the country. From that we may fairly judge the value that attaches to them, and it is very important that they should be so considered. That being so, the right hon. gentleman now says, and says very properly: I do not propose to appeal to the privy council. The judgment of the supreme court, which is indefinite in some respects and definite in others, is a judgment from which no effort will be made to appeal. That is, no application will be made for leave to appeal to the privy council, and that being so, the judgment may be taken as final and: conclusive so far as it is possible for a judgment of the supreme court to be final and conclusive.

The word "judgment" is used in our courts with respect to it. It is

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Bennett
nothing more than answers to questions, which answers are made a judgment of the court, based upon the opinion of the judges for giving the answers that are given. In the privy council as in the supreme court, the judgments thus given, the word "judgment" being used in that respect, are published in the law reports of the country. Many of the questions, notably in the companies' reference and the ones with respect to fisheries, were questions in which judgments, so-called, were given by the privy council, and the questions were answered in some instances categorically, and others in the sense that because of their vagueness, they were incapable of being answered. The closing words of Mr. Justice Duff in this case are as follows:
It is important, also, since the opinions evoked by such questions "are of course", as Lord LoTeburn states in the same passage, "only advisory, and will have no more effect than opinions of the law officers", to observe that, when a concrete case is presented for the practical application of the principles discussed, it may be found necessary, under the light derived from a survey of the facts, to modify the statement of such views as are herein expressed.
I regard those last words as being words fraught with many serious consequences to this country. They at least support the position which we suggested to the government the year before last in connection with another matter. In other words, the supreme court says: When a concrete case arises, it may be necessary from a survey of the facts to modify the statement of such views as are herein expressed. Those words are very serious-to modify the views herein expressed. The opinions of the supreme court, therefore, so far as we are concerned, may be taken as having no particular or peculiar value and do not illuminate the dark recesses of our minds with respect to the complex problem with which we have to deal.
I am not going to make complaint of the government's action in this matter except to say that I do not think they did what the provinces suggested might have been done. It will be recalled that counsel for the provinces suggested that counsel for the Dominion along with themselves might attend before the supreme court and have a preliminary discussion looking to the formulation of questions, the answers to which would be illuminating and guiding. Counsel for the Dominion did not attend.

At least Mr. Rowell and his associate were not present on that occasion and nothing further was done with regard to it. My only complaint in that regard is, that it would have been much easier to have the provincial viewpoint submitted to the court in the form of satisfactory questions than to have formulated those questions in the final form in which they were and which, in the judgment of counsel for the provinces, did not properly place the matter before the court. That is the position taken, rightly or wrongly, by counsel for the provinces.
As regards the answers to the questions in the form in which they were submitted to and considered by the court, it would not require a highly skilled lawyer to say there was not much doubt the court could not answer categorically the questions submitted to it.
My first complaint is that the provinces and the Dominion are now being asked to get together instead of having been invited to get together in the first place for the purpose of just such a conference as the right hon. gentleman now suggests in order that the questions submitted might meet every viewpoint proposed by the provincial authorities. Had that conference been held in the first place, we could have avoided the language of the jurgment, namely, that the court may modify its present opinion in the light of concrete facts. Those words detract so seriously from the value of the judgment that I consider it is of little value. If the court reserves the right to modify, vary, amend, change or alter its opinion because of further light and knowledge and concrete facts that may arise in any particular instance, the value of answers thus given I consider to be very slight.
The next point to which I desire to direct attention is that it is clear .that a treaty can be made only between the Dominion and the United States and not between the provinces and the United States. It is of the utmost importance that whatever is done in any

Just at this

As I gather it, the impression in his mind is that before we had intimated to the United States that a conference with the provinces would be necessary at the outset we had indicated to the United States that we were prepared to make an agreement. What I wanted to make clear to my hon. friend was this: Our position with the United States all along has been that we could not even discuss a treaty with them until the provinces had been called into conference with ourselves, but that before we called the provinces into conference with ourselves we wished to find out what would be an acceptable basis of negotiation. We have given no final undertaking to enter into a treaty.

If for a moment my
right hon. friend suggested that I had assumed he made any binding agreement to enter into a treaty, I relieve his mind at once; but I do submit that what he has done by the notes that have passed between his government and the government of the United States was to say that we were prepared to enter into negotiations, but that there were certain preliminary difficulties as between the provinces and the Dominion which we proposed to refer to the courts of the country for determination, and that they must first be disposed of before we would know how far we ourselves could go in making a treaty.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY DEVELOPMENT OF WATER-POWER AND IMPROVEMENT OF NAVIGATION
speechtext:
The notes themselves
give the exact language, but as they are not before me I cannot refer to them. Undoubtedly the Prime Minister indicated in his notes that he proposed that the constitutional position of the Dominion with respect to the provinces should be settled before a treaty was negotiated, but that the Dominion was ready-that was the whole essence of the notes-to enter into discussions looking towards the making of a treaty. I think that is as far as it went.. That being so, the question as to the rights of the Dominion and the rights of the provinces became of para-
mount importance. The provinces claim to own the bed of the streams, and the Dominion claim the right of navigation. To what extent the right to develop power may be a right that belongs to the provinces, in view of their alleged ownership of the water, or to what extent the power may belong to the Dominion, the question also as to the right of the Dominion to claim ownership of the power as being ancillary only to the control of navigation, are questions to which the government sought an answer, and as to which the Prime Minister said his government had not received a final determination. Because of the uncertainty in which the matter is now left, it is my judgment that it would be desirable to have first, action taken by the provinces and the Dominion that will lead to a determination of the rights in question, and, second, ratification by the proper authorities of the relative rights of the provinces and the Dominion. I wholly agree with what has been said by the Prime Minister this afternoon, namely, that before any final determination is taken even to negotiate with respect to matters of this kind, there must be, by agreement, or by judicial determination, an exact delimitation of the powers of the provinces on the one hand, and of the Dominion on the other. That is what I apprehend to be the position, and I think with that every Canadian must be in accord.
But I would remind the right hon. gentleman that it is not quite accurate to say that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec alone are concerned. I think on mature consideration the right hon. gentleman will agree that a matter that affects the national life of the country and involves, it may be, our national honour by treaty obligation, and which must affect, as it does, the western provinces, for if the shipway is to have the value that has been mentioned in times past by successive commissions and advisory councils, then indeed those who live in the western part of Canada, as well as those who reside along the lake front in Ontario and along the river front in Quebec, must be vastly interested and concerned about the ultimate result.
I am not going to do more than say this: The obligation for the formulation of any policy which results in a treaty rests with the government of the day. That is clear. It is not the function or the duty of an opposition to indicate what its views may be with respect to the matter for that responsibility rests with the administration of the day. The Prime Minister has conceded that no acceptance of that responsibility translated into concrete action will be made ef-

Chignecto Canal-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
fective unless this parliament approves. That is all this parliament might reasonably ask, namely, that before this Dominion is committed by its government to any treaty obligation the people of Canada through their representatives in parliament shall have an opportunity to express their views as to whether the treaty thus made is desirable or not.
With respect to the other matter, the question of the relative rights of the provinces and of the Dominion, it is reasonably clear in the light of the opinion to which I have referred, in its closing words, that unless the provinces have themselves agreed with the Dominion that certain action shall be taken, and indicated the form which that action shall take, then indeed a treaty otherwise negotiated and approved by this parliament would be but an invitation for future difficulties and troubles. How that approval by the provinces is to be taken, whether by resolution of their legislatures or otherwise, is not a matter that for the moment I shall discuss. It will be remembered that in the United States constitutional amendments require the various states to give their approval separately, as well as the congress of the United States. This matter affects not one province or two, but every province of confederation except British Columbia-it does not directly affect the maritime provinces, but in another sense it does, because ' if the ship-way is of the value that has been indicated in times past, it will enable them to move their products to central Canada by water rather than by rail-with the exception of British Columbia every province is vitally interested, and when the right hon. gentleman made his reference to two provinces, I presume he will modify that view to the extent of saying that all the provinces that might be interested would have the opportunity of expressing their views with respect to any arrangement that might be made.
I hardly think it was necessary to make the closing observations that he did, that any treaty negotiated would protect the interests of this country, and that it was proposed to see that it did so, because no government would endure in Canada, whether a Liberal government, a Conservative government, or some other form of government, that did not protect the interests of the Canadian people. The whole point of difference is whether or not, in the opinion of the majority either of the members of parliament or of the electors, the measures taken are measures that do adequately protect the interests of the people as a whole, and in the end the people determine that question. The government obviously must be assured that the measures they take shall be in the best interests of the Canadian people, unless it be that in this case the right hon. gentleman should suddenly change his mind and find evidence of a " thoroughly vicious principle," and come to the conclusion that the course he now proposes to pursue is one which he will then amend and change, as he saw fit to declare with respect to another matter the other day.

May I interrupt my hon. friend to ask what commission he is referring to and what is the date of the report?

The commission headed by Sir Hugh Allan, which was appointed in 1870, and reported to the government in 1871.
Quoting further the report says:
A steamer laded with flour for St. John, N.B. now goes down the gulf as far as Shediac, where the cargo is transported by rail to its destination. The total distance by water from Shediac through the Gut of Canso and around the coast of Nova Scotia to the bay of Fundy as far as the commercial capital of New Brunswick is about six hundred miles, and the consequence is that there is little or no direct communication between the bay of Fundy ports and those of the river St. Lawrence. By a canal through the isthmus the distance from Shediac to St. John will not be much more than one hundred miles.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, the government of the day decided to proceed with the con* struction of the canal. His Excellency Lord Dufferin, at the opening of the session of 1873, in the speech from the throne used the following language, which may be found on page 2 of the parliamentary debates of that year:
I am glad to inform you that plans and specifications for the enlargement of the Welland, and the construction of the Baie Verte canal, have been completed, and that the works can now be put under contract. The surveys for the St. Lawrence canals will, I am assured, be finished in time to commence the works at the beginning of next year. This will insure the completion of all these great works at the same period.
In accordance with the promise thus given in the speech from the throne $1,000,000 was placed in the estimates that year for the construction of the Bade Verte canal which, according to the late Mr. Page's estimate of the line surveyed by Messrs. Gzowski and Keefer, was to cost between seven and eight million dollars.
In 1875 another commission was appointed, with the late Hon. John Young as chairman.
The report made by this commission was unfavourable. The Hon. Joseph Lawrence, however, one of the commissioners, protested against the verdict of the majority and in a separate minority report ably defended the commercial prospects of the canal. After a complete and thorough survey of the whole matter he summed up his conclusions as follows:
Having given to the trust delegated to me, as one of the canal commission of 1875, the most careful and studious attention, I would recommend to the government, in the interests of the Dominion, the construction of a full tide canal, of the size designated in this report, believing it to be adequate to all the exigencies of commerce, at least for many years. It is a matter, however, meriting the consideration of the government, as to whether the suggestion of Professor Hind, for a tidal highway, might not be adopted, for, should it be found not to meet the requirements of trade, it could be made into a canal.
It is a work which Sir Hugh Allan, Gzowski, Calvin. Gavreau, Jardine, Shannon and Keefer declared "was essential to give unity and completeness to the canal system of the country, and was Canadian in design, and must prove national in its results." With my colleagues. I most cordially join in "the hope that the existing depression in business will prove temporary, and that with increasing population, and the extension of the industry of the country, the progress of the future will be equal to the past, and this will be greatly stimulated by the cheapening of transit from all points of the interior to the consumers of the east, and to the ports of shipment to Europe." To the attainment of these patriotic aspirations, what will do more than a connection of the waters of the bay of Fundy with the waters of the gulf of St. Lawrence?
In the report of the second canal commission, reporting in 1875, it was discovered that there was an error in the computation of the distance to be saved by the shore cut. The commissioners had represented the distance saved from Montreal to St. John as only 225 miles, whereas it is actually 500 miles, making an error in that respect in their calculation of 275 miles. The prejudice produced in some quarters by the misrepresentation of the distance saved-and hence some of the erroneous conclusions of the report-endures in the east to this day.
With respect to the adverse report, may I point out that certain admissions were made. I should like briefly to refer to one paragraph in this respect. It is stated:
The evidence taken, and the observations which the commissioners have had the opportunity of making, have impressed them deeply with the vast resources of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and the large increase which may reasonably be looked for in their trade and commerce.
May I now quote a rather lengthy resolution which was adopted by the Amherst Board

Chignecto Canal-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
of Trade on September 12, 1928, which I think covers quite thoroughly the salient points of this whole scheme:
Whereas numerous surveys of the route to connect the waters of the gulf of St. Lawrence with those of the bay of Fundy by cutting across the isthmus of Chignecto were made between the years 1825 and 1864, and
Whereas at the Quebec conference held in 1864 "it was distinctly understood and agreed" that the carnal would be built if confederation were consummated, and
Whereas in 1870 the federal government appointed a commission of eminent men to examine into the canal projects of Canada, which commission held meetings and examined witnesses in Halifax, St. John, Quebec, Ottawa, Kingston, Belleville, Toronto, Hamilton, London. Stratford, Guelph and Windsor in Canada, and Chicago, Milwaukee, Detroit, Toledo and Oswego in the United States, and received reports from the corporate towns and public meetings, and
Whereas this canal commission reported in 1871 and divided the proposed works of Canada into four classes, and set forth:
"that all the works embraced under the head of first class are really of so great importance, so essential to the welfare and prosperity of the whole country, that they should be undertaken and proceeded with," and
Whereas in reference to the canal across the isthmus of Chignecto the report reads as follows:-[DOT]
"Inseparably connected *with the growth of intercolonial trade in the construction of the Bay Yerte canal, across the isthmus of Chignecto connecting the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The advantages that must accrue, not merely to the Dominion as a whole, but to the commerce of the maritime provinces, are so clearly pointed out by the boards of trade of all the leading cities of Canada, and by men interested in the development of our commercial interests, not simply the merchants of St. John and other places in the locality of the proposed eanal but merchants of Hamilton, Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal and Quebec, that it is superfluous for the commissioners to do more than briefly refer to a few salient features of the scheme."
"The total distance by water from Shediac through the Gut of Canso and around the coast of Nova Scotia to the bay of Fundy as far as the commercial capital of New Brunswick is about 600 miles and the consequence is that there is little or no direct communication between the bay of Fundy ports and those of the river St. Lawrence. By a canal through the isthmus the distance from Shediac to St. John will not be much more than one hundred miles. This fact will show the insuperable obstacle that now exists to anything like extensive commerce between Montreal and the bay of Fundy ports of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and the great impulse that must be necessarily given to trade by the opening up of a route which will shorten the distance so considerably, furnish an inland navigation from the Lakes to Boston, and consequently lessen freights between these points.
When we consider the shorter distance and the lessening of insurance in the autumn on account of a safer route than that now taken through Canso and round the Atlantic coast of Nova Scotia, so exposed at certain seasons to fogs and storms, etc. etc.

The lumber and fishery interests of the gulf of St. Lawrence both of the island of Prince Edward, and what is generally known as the north shore of New Brunswick, will also be benefited by their being afforded a safer and shorter route not only to the ports of the bay of Fundy but also to those of the northeastern coast of the United States.
It will enable the valuable stones of the quarries, the olive freestone of Dorchester, the gypsum of Hants and Hillsborough, the grind and scythe stones in the vicinity of Cumberland bay, and as well the albertite of New Brunswick, which is unsurpassed for illuminating purposes, to be transported to the Canadian market from which it is now virtually shut off by the difficulty and cost of transit.
The St. John, N.B. Chamber of Commerce states the benefits arising from the construction of this canal as follows:-
1.	The maritime provinces import, say 700,000 barrels of flour annually, besides a great many other articles of bulky character.
2.	The maritime provinces possess inexhaustible supplies of productions required by Ontario and Quebec.
3.	The chief articles of import from Ontario to the maritime provinces, and vice versa, being bulky, the element of freight forms a large item in their value; hence, any greater facility for transit tending to cheapen the cost must be productive of a greatly increased demand.
4.	This canal would not only afford the desired facility for transit by rendering it unnecessary to break bulk between the points of shipment and destination, but would remove a great barrier to cheap freights by enabling owners of vessels to secure cargoes to Ontario and Quebec and thus build up a mutually desirable reciprocal trade, which may be increased to almost any extent.

Whereas there is more need for the canal to-day than there was in 1871 for the purpose of interprovineial trade and particularly for the conveying of produce from Bay of Fundy ports to the markets of central Canada, including apples from the Annapolis and Cornwallis valleys, coal from the Cumberland coal basin, gypsum from the counties of Hants and Albert, and granite from Charlotte and Shelburne, and
Whereas the construction of this canal would lessen the distance by water from Prince Edward Island to St. John, N.B., by nearly 400 miles and would give potatoes and other products of that island much cheaper rates by water transportation particularly to the ports of the United States along the Atlantic seaboard, and
