Whereas it would lessen the distance by water between Ontario and Quebec and the port of St. John, N.B., by several hundred miles, and provide a coastal trade in which could be used boats which would navigate the canals of central Canada so that goods could be transported without breaking bulk, and
Whereas it would shorten the distance from points in northern Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island as well as from ports on the eastern coast of New Brunswick and the ports of the St. Lawrence river to the British West Indies and to Cuba, and
Whereas the total length of the canal would be only about eighteen miles, and would pass, according to the engineers' reports, except for the distance of less than a mile, through soft material.
Therefore resolved the Dominion government be requested to proceed with the construction of this canal at the earliest possible date.
Resolutions similar to this were passed by a number of boards of trade all over the martime provinces; I have some of them here but will not weary the house by reading them. However, I would like to mention one in particular, a resolution passed by the Spring-78594- 28
hill board of trade stressing the fact that the canal would be of considerable advantage to them in the shipment of their coal to Parrsboro then up to bay of Fundy through the proposed canal to the Montreal market.
I also wish to say that a resolution was passed at Halifax last year by the maritime board of trade, a body made up of all the associated boards of trade of the maritime provinces. It is non-political, dealing with various non-political matters and passing resolutions from time to time in favour of or condemning certain projects mooted in the maritime provinces. This project has received the wholehearted support of the maritime board of trade, although I am bound to add that the resolution passed by that body is not so strong as the one I have just read, in that it asks the federal government to investigate, by a survey and by modern, expert engineering opinion, this proposed canal to ascertain if the scheme is considered practicable.
I also have here some correspondence from different firms all over the maritime provinces with respect to the benefits which will be derived from the construction of this proposed canal. Most of the correspondence en-r larges on the matters to which I have already referred, and points out the distinct advantage to the general trade of the three maritime provinces which would result from the construction of this canal. The possibilities of increased trade between the maritime provinces .and the rest of Canada have not been developed in a corresponding or relative measure with the rest of the Dominion, due in part to a lack of adequate transportation facilities and geographical handicaps which place us to-day in a position of inequality since we do not fully participate in whatever measure of prosperity is being enjoyed by other portions of the country. We must remember that from the time of confederation up to March 31, 1928, we have spent $266,828752.80 on the construction, maintenance, staff and repairs of the canals of Canada, while only $1,737,425.10 has been spent in the maritime provinces, on what is known as the St. Peter's canal in Cape Breton. So it does not occur to me that our request at this time is unreasonable or inopportune. I would point out further that when the Bale Verte canal scheme was revived by the Amherst board of trade last year we were delighted with the response from different parts of the country and from the newspapers of Canada. I have not time to read them all, but as an example I wish to quote from the Montreal Herald of July 26, 1928:

434	COMMONS
Chignecto Canal-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
The memories of most of us do not go back fifty years to the time when the Baie Verte canal project was a live political issue. We venture to prophesy, however, that, before a tiny portion of the next half century passes, the people of Canada will become aware of where and what this canal was and meant. In short, the Baie Verte canal scheme is now re-christened the Chignecto canal proposal, and the maritimes, discarding party politics, are showing a determined spirit to demonstrate to the rest of Canada its advantages and to stir the federal government to father the project.
H. J. Logan is one of the active promoters and one need know nothing more about Mr. Logan than the success of his efforts to revive our West Indies trade to realize that there is likely to be a stirring of the waters in good earnest.
Our readers will want to know what this Chignecto canal project is and means. We cover the subject briefly.
_ Chignecto bay and Cumberland basin give into each other at the head of the bay of Fundy. A fraction over 20 miles separates these waters from Baie Verte, an arm of Northumberland strait. The Chignecto canal will connect Cumberland basin and Baie Verte.
The country through which the construction would be carried on would present no great difficulties, and we believe the cost would be but a small fraction of any one of our other canal expenditures.
We would not be so greatly interested were the idea one that would be of sole benefit to the maritimes. Brief study only is needed, however, to convince that this is not a local or provincial concern, but one of national import.
It would shorten the distance by water from Prince Edward Island ports to Saint John and United States Atlantic ports by six hundred miles, and save the cost of breaking bulk and reshipment by rail.
It would shorten the distance by water from Montreal to bay of Fundy by five hundred miles, and to the West Indies by 400 miles. These distances mean a saving of two days- an important matter.
Apples from the land of Evangeline; coal from Cumberland, and gypsum from Hants; olive freestone from Dorchester; the grind and scythe stones from Cumberland; and albertite, unsurpassed for illuminating purposes, from New Brunswick, could be carried to the markets of central Canada at small cost.
The Saint John, N.B., chamber of commerce sums up the advantages as follows:-
_ "This canal would not only afford the desired facility for transit by rendering it unnecessary to break bulk between the points of shipment and destination, but would remove a great barrier to cheap freights by enabling owners of vessels to secure return cargoes to Ontario and Quebec, and thus build up a mutually desirable reciprocal trade, which may be increased to almost any extent."
Here is something good for the maritimes and for Canada. Every Montreal citizen, no matter what his origin, can give his support unhesitatingly. It is specially a project that the Maritime Provinces Club of Montreal, recently organized, might get behind with all the weight of the great influence of its membership.

The maritimes may count on the unwavering support of the Montreal Herald, if party politics is left out of their efforts to make this dream come true.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.
Mr. SMITH (Cumberland); Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock, I had just concluded reading an extract from the Montreal Herald endorsing this project. In the concluding paragraph it stated that it would give it unwavering support if party politics were left out. I believe that can be answered to the complete satisfaction of all. The resolution of the Amherst board of trade read by me this afternoon was moved by the Hon. H. J. Logan, a recent and very popular appointment by the government to the Senate of Canada. Mr. Logan for some time past has taken a very keen interest in this project and is one of those instrumental in having the matter revived. The project has also been endorsed unanimously by the Maritime Board of Trade, a non-political organization in every sense, representing as it does all the local boards of trade of the three maritime provinces, to the extent of asking the government to ascertain as to the feasibility of the project. Many of the press of all political shades have endorsed the scheme, so that I believe this is one measure of which it can be truthfully said is stripped of all political colouring.
May I, in conclusion, draw to the attention of the house once more the fact that away back in 1871 the project was thoroughly considered by a commission whose personnel was of a highly responsible type of Canadian *citizens of capacity and vision, and after a thorough and most exhaustive investigation they recommended that a canal across the isthmus of Chignecto was a transportation necessity from a national viewpoint, to complete the system of canals in Canada for the purpose of stimulating interprovincial trade, to alleviate existing geographical handicaps and also to promote further our commercial possibilities? Is it not fitting to say now that if there was reason for their favourable recommendations in the seventies, surely after upwards of fifty years progress along commercial and transportation lines, the national advantages and economic necessities are correspondingly greater in these days of speed, short cuts and elimination of geographical obstacles? This canal, if constructed, will not only serve the various interests of Canada I have mentioned, but have a far-reaching tendency to

Chignecto Canal-Mr. MacLaren
stimulate and develop commerce and tonnage through new channels, and develop trade, the greatest benefits of which can only now be visualized but the realities of which may be realized when the project is consummated and in operation.
On the various grounds I have mentioned I appeal to all members of the house to pass the resoluton which I take pleasure in moving, seconded by the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. MacLaren), asking the government of Canada to further investigate the project with the least possible delay, as to feasibility; cost of construction; economic, provincial and national advantage to be gained; and, when these have been satisfactorily established, that the government take the necessary steps to proceed with the construction of the canal at the earliest possible date.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for
Cumberland (Mr. Smith) has given the house a comprehensive account of the project called the Baie Verte canal. It is a subject that has been before the house on several occasions during the past number of years; but for various reasons the proposal has not been proceeded with, although, as hon. members will remember, at one time a sum was actually voted for carrying out the work. One important reason for stopping this project was a fantastic proposal to build a ship railway which was actually started but not completed, the result being that the unfortunate, unsuccessful proposal of building a ship railway has delayed the matter very seriously until we have arrived at the present time.
A new interest has now arisen, and a desire is becoming general that this proposal of the Baie Verte canal, so called, be now carried out. The province of Nova Scotia is connected wth the province of New Brunswick by what is called the Chignecto isthmus, which is a narrow isthmus varying from eighteen to twenty miles in width. Were the canal constructed, it would bring into contact two large bodies of water, the strait of Northumberland and the bay of Fundy. It would result in the ports of Prince Edward Island being approximated by some hundreds of miles to ports along the bay of Fundy and ports of the United States. It would also have a similar effect on the ports of the north shore of New Brunswick and the north shore of Nova Scotia, in all those cases there being a saving of some hundreds of miles. It is estimated that, by the construction of this canal, something like 500 miles would be saved in the distance between ports of the river St. Lawrence, Quebec 7S594-28J
and Montreal, and St. John and other ports on the bay of Fundy, and ports such as Portland, Maine, Boston and New York.
There are several outstanding points of interest in this connection. First of all there is the fact that it would be a short canal, being something less than twenty miles. The next point is the cost of construction. The soil can be easily removed and the quantity of rock is quite small. Another point is, in comparison with the short canal, the great saving of mileage between the strait of Northumberland and the bay of Fundy. This motion recommends that a survey be made of the area where the canal might be built, and that a report be made as to its feasibility and whether it would be a sound economic proposition; and should the report be favourable, the motion recommends that the construction of the canal be proceeded with. That seems to me a fair proposition. Personally I believe that such a canal would be of very great service to the shipping trade in that portion of the country, and I trust that the government will look upon this matter favourably and agree to the motion being passed.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals):	Mr. SpeakeT, the
matter of a canal in the location referred to in the resolution of my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Smith) has been, as he has stated, brought actively to the attention of the government during the past year, notably by Senator Hance LogaD, and I have had the advantage of hearing from the senator many of the arguments which my hon. friend has advanced this afternoon and this evening.
The proposal is an old one, dating back to before confederation. I have been interested enough to delve somewhat into its history, and I find that there was a canal commission appointed in 1870 to report on the importance of inland navigation generally throughout Canada, a commission which dealt with the then existing canals and waterways and a number of other projects, including the one referred to in the resolution. The report of the commissioners, which was made in the following year, 1871, recommended this project at an estimated cost of $3,250,000 at that time, providing for locks two hundred and seventy feet in length, forty feet in width, and fifteen feet draught on the mitre sills. In passing, I might remark that in all probability a study would reveal that the dimensions provided for in the report of 1870 would not be adequate to-day. At any rate that question would require very careful examination.

Chignecto Canal-Mr. Dunning
Those dimensions would be useless.

From a mere glance at the figures I am inclined to agree with my hon. friend, that they would be useless to provide adequate accommodation under modern conditions. In 1873 a report was made on the project by John Page, then chief engineer of the Department of Public Works, apparently on the same basis of dimensions. He reported the probable cost of the canal to be $7,100,000. The matter was further considered by the government of that time, and a second royal commission was appointed. My hon. friend from Cumberland has referred to that, and has read some extracts from the minority report which was presented by one of the members of that second commission. But the fact remains that this second royal commission, which reported to the Secretary of State on December 2, 1875, stated that it was not in the interests of the Dominion that the proposed canal should be constructed. I shall not go over the ground that my hon. friend covered in that connection. The commission reported, with the exception of one member, as I have just indicated.
In 1882, the company referred to by my hon. friend from St. John-Albert (Mr. MacLaren) was incorporated to construct a marine railway across the peninsula, having as part of its financial basis a subsidy payable by the federal government with respect to the operation of the railway once it was completed. After a somewhat hectic career, this company entirely ceased operations.

It did a good deal of
work, though, first.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with practically everything that has been said by the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) I am wholly in accord. One of the earliest recollections of my political life was a discussion with a gentleman who represented certain interests that were undertaking to build a marine railway across the isthmus of Chignecto. As a consequence of that discussion I made some inquiries as to how the project came into being, and it was apparent that at one time the country did contemplate the construction of a canal across that isthmus. It was not carried forward. Under modern conditions, with improvements such as we have to-day, it may well be that we can construct such a canal for practically the same cost that was estimated in the first instance.
I saw some of the old ship railway canal construction work last summer, and I took the trouble to learn something of the onetime proposed location of the canal. Certainly it is a problem that has been engaging the attention of men and women from the maritime provinces for a long time as to how the waters of the straits of Northumberland might be connected with those of the bay of Fundy, thereby improving transportation facilities and decreasing the cost of the movement of freight from the lower provinces to the upper provinces and from the upper provinces to the lower, and even to the United States.
The minister has promised to give this matter the attention that has been suggested by the member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith) in the resolution, and I think this will commend itself to every part of the country, and I am sure it does to this house. I rather concur with his suggestion that the hon. gentleman withdraw the last paragraph of the resolution, for I am free to say I quite agree with the minister that an antecedent commitment by parliament to any course of action dependent upon a satisfactory report is too vague and indefinite, because what might be satisfactory to my hon. friend to-day might not be entirely so to his successor to-morrow. It might well be that some "vicious principle" would make it inadvisable to proceed with what the government thought to be sound a week before. Judging from the studied care with which the hon. minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) is now observing his reports, I am satisfied that he would not regard it as a "vicious principle" that this work should be undertaken by the Department of Railways and Canals, and not by the department over which he presides.

Mr. Speaker,
I think the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith) is to be congratulated on bringing this matter before the house. Of the three maritime provinces, probably Prince Edward Island is the most interested in this project. The fact that the survey was made away back in 1870 and nothing has been done in the meantime to carry out the work does not prove that such a work is not a necessity. As has been very well pointed out, even if it were not a necessity in the past, with the great increase in production of the maritime provinces, with the consequent need of more extended markets at the present time, this work is positively of greater concern to us now than it ever was.
A glance at the map that has been laid on our desks shows that a direct route would be opened up between Prince Edward Island and the ports of St. John and Boston, thus effecting a saving of a few hundred miles and to that extent reducing our cost of transportation and expediting deliveries. To-day we are more handicapped in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia and New Brunswick than we have been for a number of years with respect to markets for our agricultural products. The very fact that we are developing our trade with the West Indies and with Cuba makes it all the more imperative that this work should be gone ahead with in order to give us the cheapest transportation possible for our agricultural products, particularly in view of the possibility that the United States may through certain upward tariff revisions which are now pending intimate that they do not want to trade with us.
Cheap transportation is of vital concern to us in the maritime provinces. During the past year we1 had a large surplus crop of potatoes, which are bringing a very, very low price. Last season the Dominion Stores desired to place an order for two hundred carloads of Prince Edward Island potatoes. As hon. members are aware, there are freight zones throughout the Dominion, the freight rates to any particular point varying in each of those zones. As a result of a difference of about five dollars a car, the zones furthest away from the point of destination could not secure any of that two-hundred-car order although the difference in the cost was only 85 per car. That is one case that came directly to our notice last season. Therefore it will be seen what an advantage cheaper transportation would be to Prince Edward Island, for it would give us extended markets, and even $5 per car often means the moving of the crop or not moving it.
438	COMMONS
Chiynecto Canal-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
But in addition to our agricultural markets we require a market for our fish. Probably the best fishing grounds of the whole Atlantic are off our shores. On the north side of the island we have a very important cod-fishing industry, but up to the present it has never been developed in a profitable way. Some day someone is going to wake up to the possibilities of that great industry, and it will be so organized and developed that a larger market will be absolutely necessary for the products of this industry as well as for lobsters, scallops and other sea foods.
Hon. members may be surprised when I state that right in the province of Prince Edward Island if we had a short canal connecting the north side of the island with Northumberland straits it would do more for the province and for its fishing industry than perhaps anything else that we could devise. There is one point between Richmond bay and Bedeque bay where tidewater is only separated by about four miles. A canal cut through that narrow part would allow all the north shore of Prince Edward Island to be in direct communication with railway and cold storage facilities, and with the shipping facilities that the south side already enjoys. I do not know whether this matter has ever before been brought up, but the people of the north side of the province are asking for railway connection. This is one way of solving their problems. Last year the people on the north side of the island chartered schooners and loaded them with agricultural products and sent them an a voyage of one hundred miles around the north cape and down the south side of the island to Summerside habour where the cargo was transshipped to steamers there loading for the southern states. That is a hardship and an expense which the agricultural people of that community cannot bear. Why not investigate this needed work at the same time as the mainland scheme is being investigated. I am throwing this out as a suggestion as to what might be done. We were told this afternoon that a sum of over $266,000,000 has been expended on canals throughout Canada. Not one dollar of that money has ever been spent in the province from which I have the honour to come; and no doubt, as the development of canals throughout the country will continue, Prince Edward Island will be contributing in the future, as it has done in the past, to these public works from which the people in that province have been reaping no benefits themselves. I am offering this suggestion as one which in my opinion should be considered in connection with this project which is before

the house at the present time. The linking up of the north shore of Prince Edward Island directly with the south side will provide facilities which are greatly needed, and if this work of the Chignecto canal goes on we shall be put into close touch with St. John, Boston and other markets. As has been pointed out, this work has been endorsed by the maritime boards of trade and by every public body in the maritime provinces. I feel sure, from what the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) has said, that the matter will be given careful consideration, and I trust that at some future date we shall see this important work pushed forward to a satisfactory conclusion.

I
am in full accord with the proposal of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith). It is true that to-day canals are not viewed as being of that degree of importance which they were fifty years ago. That is due largely to the great improvement which has been effected in railway transportation. Nevertheless, canals have their place, and in that connection I wish to point out, what has already been referred to, that while we in Canada have spent some $260,000,000 odd in canal construction, improvement and maintenance, of that vast sum but less than three-quarters of a million has been spent in the three maritime provinces. In view of that, I submit that the proposal which the hon. member for Cumberland has made should receive the support of all members of the house. I am quite in accord with the suggestion made by the Minister of Railways, that locks such as were considered by the power commissioners who investigated the project would be totally inadequate; they would be useless. If that canal is to be built, the lock would need to be not less than 500 feet in length with at least 25 feet depth on the sills. There is no use proposing or constructing anything under those dimensions, if modem steamers are to go through the cut.
Would my hon. friend consider 25 feet on the sills sufficient under modern conditions?
I suggested that as the minimum.
I agree with my hon. friend.

They should be 30 to 33 feet. The canal should have locks of equal capacity with those on the St. Lawrence, whatever may be ultimately decided upon.

Chignecto Canal-Mr. Cantley
Twenty-seven feet in depth and provision for thirty feet in the locks.

Exactly. Now, I do not think I need say very much more regarding the proposal, in view of the statement made by the minister. I take it he is speaking on behalf of the government, who are prepared to go on with the investigation.
I assume therefore that the mover will meet the minister's suggestion and drop the last clause of the resolution. A good deal could be said on the subject, but I do not think it now necessary.
Reviewing the history of the ship railway which was proposed by Sir Charles Tupper,
I believe, so far as my memory goes, that it was the only project with which his name was associated in the development of Canada which was not carried through to a final and successful conclusion. In my opinion the whole scheme of the ship railway was wrong in essence and principle. I do not think there was any warrant for it; as it would compare in usefulness with a modern canal system such as is now proposed. The proposal, in connection with the ship railway, was to dock the vessels, raise them on a cradle and transport them across the isthmus, the railway for this purpose consisting of four bands of parallel standard gauge track laid with 110 pound steel. The dock was completed on one side and partially completed on the other. The machinery for lifting the vessels out of the water on the southern side was installed. The rails were laid over a considerable portion of the road. Subsequently the whole plant was scrapped; the rails were lifted and most were taken to New Glasgow, where the great bulk of them were re-melted. That was practically the end of the enterprise. As pointed out by the Minister of Railways, some considerable losses were sustained and claims made. The charter was extended on two occasions, but the project ultimately fell through.
I take it that, so far as the present proposal of the member for Cumberland is concerned, the government will see that an investigation is made. What the result will be remains to be seen, but I know that it will be viewed with a considerable degree of satisfaction in the maritime provinces, that an investigation is to be made. I leave the matter at that.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
After the statement by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) as to the attitude of the government in connection with the project under consideration, it is necessary for one to discuss the merits of the question, because that is the very essence of the investigation which it is proposed to make, namely, that the merits shall be thoroughly gone into, the economic situation examined, and all the information brought to bear which would assist in arriving at a conclusion as to the national advantage, the practical utility, and the economic possibility of the scheme.
My purpose in rising is perhaps a very personal one. The project happens to be put forward primarily by the citizens of my native town of Amherst. My hon. friend, the member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith), this afternoon read certain resolutions from the town council of Amherst. This brings back to my mind recollections of early days. Probably I had a more intimate association with the so-called ship railway, or Chignecto marine railway, than even the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). I want to tell him that I drove a bread wagon which supplied bread for the navvies who worked on that particular job.
I feel therefore that I know a good deal at first hand about the ship railway. It was with regret to mj'self as well as to the older citizens that the project was discontinued. Let me say for my fellow citizens of Amherst, that they are not the sort of people who just ask governments to do things. The citizens of Amherst are the kind of people who have tried to help themselves. There were a good many industries in that town-flourishing industries which were promoted in no small measure by the money, the energy and the courage of the people of Amherst. It was and is a matter of regret to us all that some of those industries are not in the prosperous condition in which we should like to see them. The citizens of Amherst have received a good many hard blows in connection with development there, but they still look forward and this is a project in which they are taking a real and definite interest. They are going about it in a dignified and logical way, but energetically nevertheless. They are not asking impossibilities; they are asking that the matter be first thoroughly investigated in the light of present day conditions and they are basing their request upon the fact that a great many years ago a commission did make findings favourable to the construction of the canal. There was, as the hon. member (Mr. Smith) has pointed out, a later commission which made a finding rather the reverse of that, and the project was allowed to lapse, whether on account of the proposal of the Chignecto marine ' railway or whether because of other reasons I do not know. However, I feel that with

Chignecto Canal-Mr. Ralston
citizens and public bodies like these asking parliament for examination and consideration it is only fair and right thalt what is set out in the second last paragraph of this resolution should be granted and a full inquiry made. As a former resident of the county of Cumberland. in which is also the thriving town of Springhil'l mentioned by my hon. friend this afternoon, which of course would be interested, and in which are also other enterprising and active towns, I am glad indeed to be a member of the government which undertakes to say that the fullest investigation will be made into this question.

Having received the assurance of the Minister of Railways, I am willing to consent to the deletion of the last paragraph of the resolution, of course on condition that the investigation into the feasibility, the cost of construction and the advantages to be gained by building this canal will be undertaken by the government with the least possible delay.

I want it made quite clear that I cannot promise to start to-morrow; my hon. friend- appreciates that fact, but having regard to the other work which the type of men needed for this investigation are presently engaged in, I am sure my hon. friend will appreciate that we will get at it as soon as we possibly can, having regard to those conditions.
The hon. gentleman cannot amend his own motion. Mr. Barber will move, seconded by Mr. Brady, that the resolution be amended by striking out the last paragraph.

Amendment agreed to.
Motion as amended agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to support the motion of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Woodsworth). Perhaps it will be interesting to the house if I quote the epigram to which he has referred in regard to the common and the goose. It is a piece of old English wit that goes back many centuries to the time when the landlords were enclosing the commons. It runs like this:
It is bad enough in man or woman
To steal the goose from off the common;
But surely he is without excuse
Who steals the common from the goose.

Natural Resources-Mr. Bird
The process of stealing the common from
the goose is going on apace in this country. In Manitoba during the last twelve months we have lost one of our most valuable public possessions and neither this parliament nor the legislature of Manitoba were able to make a protest or institute an investigation until the common had been taken away from the goose.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I submit that for any government, no matter whether Dominion or provincial, to give away our natural wealth by order in council is a usurpation of the proper functions of parliament. Why not tax by order in council-why not increase the income tax by order in council; why not increase the tariff by order in council? Why not sign treaties by order in council? Why not legislate by order in council? Why not hand government over to some Mussolini without condescending to call together the representatives of the people? There is no logic or justice in the procedure whatsoever. Why, what is the difference between depriving the people of their property by taxation and depriving them by alienating their natural wealth? There is absolutely no difference in principle. Yet in the one case our whole parliamentary system has been built up on the basis of shielding the people from arbitrary taxation. In the other case, right up to the present time, cabinets in the dim seclusion of the council chamber can give away the people's wealth to the value of hundreds of millions of dollars.
It is a long time since governments attempted to tax the people by order in council. When Charles Stuart.-I mean King Charles Stuart-levied ship money by order in council, it led to a case of amputation in a very short time. I do not want to see the present Charles Stewart suffer anything like the same fate, but there is an execution impending in the province of Manitoba. Surely we are of the same Anglo-Saxon stock; surely the same blood runs in our veins as ran in the veins of Pym and Hampden; surely we are not going to suffer our wealth to be frittered away by a committee of parliament in the recesses of the council chamber without having the opportunity to utter one word of protest.
It may have been a very harmless practice years ago before the people of Canada awakened to a sense of the vast importance of their natural wealth. When a water-power was just a matter of scenic beauty, when an oil field was just a potential sheep pasture, and a pulp forest a muskeg, it die! not matter very much whether our natural resources were administered in one way or the other, there

was nothing very serious implicated; but in recent years, particularly since the war, our natural resources have assumed a value that our grandfathers could not have imagined. We have come to a sense of our advantages as a country. Our national pride is constantly appealed to on the basis of the wonderful wealth that lies to our hands. Moreover, in every farm home, in every labourer's cottage, this sense of our common wealth has raised visions of a higher standard of Canadian life accessible to all, visions of the burden of taxation lifted, visions of domestic drudgery taken away. These visions have arisen in the minds of the men and women of Canada, and I say to this government or to any government, they are risking their very existence by tampering with this God-given wealth which belongs to the ten millions of people of Canada, and not to any government or privileged few. It is the business of governments to see that those visions are materialized, to see that these water-powers, with all this hidden wealth of forest and mine are somehow diverted into the lives of the common people, and not frittered away by unseen and secret methods to the money lords of this country and of the United States. Stripped of its traditional dignity, the government is but a committee of parliament; and I say that parliament is playing with fire when it allows governments to give away secretly the natural wealth of this country. By so doing it is creating forces and setting up influences which some day will turn and enslave parliament itself, if indeed they are not already doing so.
The nearest parallel to what is going on in Canada which I can find anywhere in history occurred about the time that little rhyme originated about four hundred years ago. The people of merrie England in the sixteenth century, in pre-Elizabethan times, owned the commons; an illimitable expanse of fertile land belonged to the inhabitants of England. But at that time the landlords began to absorb that natural resource; they began to fence it in and acquire it. Hence arose the saying that the commons were being taken away from the goose. That was four hundred years ago. As one in whom English blood runs more or less completely, I am always proud to think of old Bob Ket and his brother Bill, who in the sixteenth century rose up in their township of Wymondham in Norfolk, England, and protested against parliament allowing the landlords to absorb the commons. I can picture Bob Ket pulling

Natural Resources-Mr. Bird
down the fences of Sergeant Flowerdew. I can imagine his taking his sixteen thousand tatterdemalions to Mousehold Heath.
Years ago I stood on the very place, of which the immortal Barrow said, "There's a wind on the heath, brother". And there was more than a wind on the heath; there was something more spiritual than the wind that blew. There was something that had been agitated centuries back, and which aill down the centuries had its influence on East Anglia. That is the neighbourhood where Cromwell got his Ironsides to withstand Charles Stuart; and even to this day you can find the influence of Bob Ket working in Norfolk and Suffolk in England, because they dared four centuries ago to stand up against the encroachments of landlordism. The historian Pollock says that these men were all of very simple spirit, religious minded people, and in the manifesto which they made out they told the people of England that they regarded the enclosure of common lands as theft from the community; and they innocently considered that the gifts of God in nature belonged equally to the peasant as to the landlord. That is what these humble people meant in their rebellion four hundred years ago. And they were not left to stand alone. Poor and ragged and simple though they were, we are told that the famous Bishop Latimer stood up and said on their behalf, "These landlords are endosers, grabbers, rent raisers"; and he told his congregation that there was more cruelty, injustice, and pride in the landlords of his day than among the inhabitants of Nebo. I sometimes listen to the modern pulpit, and I think it would be a good thing if it came out of the vacuum which it has created around itself and addressed itself to some of these injustices which obtain in our time, as Bishop Latimer as well as the Roman Catholic clergy and laymen did in their time. In this way the blight of landlordism settled in England and on English institutions and government for the next three hundred years. There was a period of three hundred years of sterility for the common people of England because landlordism was clamped upon the country as we have seen.
Now to-day we are passing through a parallel process. Moneylordism is foisting itself on our free institutions in this country. As president Wilson said some years ago, there has risen up behind the forms of democracy an invisible government; it is the government of money kings, who seek privileges from parliament, whose cupidity has been stirred by the vast natural resources of the country, and who have been encouraged by the servility of governments-encouraged by our system, whereby grants of our natural resources do not come up for consideration by the people's representatives but are passed upon in the secrecy of the cabinet council. I say it is a serious thing for parliament. Parliaments, provincial and Dominion, are creating influences which some day will have them completely in possession, if they have not them in possession at the present time.
Discussion in parliament is the only means by which we can create a healthy public opinion on any question. True, discussion in parliament is not a perfect piece of procedure; we are all guilty at one time or another of indulging in talk which is unprofitable. We all do our best, and we have the best of intentions, but we sometimes waste time and bring this institution into momentary contempt. Nevertheless it is on the floor of the house that public opinion is moulded, if it is moulded at all, in the interest of the people. Oh, you will say, what about the press? What about all the agencies that are at work to build up an enlightened and intelligent public capable of taking care of its own concerns? Surely, it will be said, people do not depend upon parliament so much as they used to. Well, let me tell you of an experience we had in Manitoba with the press in connection with the Seven Sisters falls. In Manitoba we have a great newspaper which laughingly calls itself free. Not Mr. Bracken, but the Free Press is the guilty party. That great newspaper, which has insinuated its way into the confidence of the people in the last few years, and not altogether unworthily, is responsible to-day for Manitoba having lost its most valuable natural resource. Without the Free Press Mr. Bracken would not have had one printed word of support. The Grain Growers Guide, now called the Country Guide, refused to say a word in support of him-one of the most significant things you could think of. But the Free Press, the organ of light and liberty, immediately got behind Mr. Bracken the moment they saw that Mr. Bracken was get-getting behind the Winnipeg electric. The editor of that great journal is a big man with a big brain, which he does not always use fairly and squarely. This gentleman who in his editorials talks in imitation of a Greek oracle; this Manitoba king maker and king-breaker-and I say that almost literally, because I think he would have broken Mackenzie King two or three years ago if he coulfi, and when he found he could not do so he filled his editorials with all the fulsome terms he could get out of the

Natural Resources-Mr. Bird
dictionary-this potentate in Manitoba, with his million dollar press, rides rough shod over every humble expression of opinion in Manitoba differing from his own. A short time ago at a farmers' convention I daied criticize the Free Press, in my humble way; immediately the million dollar mechanism started working and crushed the life out of poor me. That is what we are up . against in Manitoba, a paper which has worked its way into the hearts of the peoiple largely through its own advocacy, but when the people's rights are in the balance it flings itself on the side of the interests.
You say the press is a noble organ of public opinion; we cannot believe that in Manitoba. We leaned on a broken reed and it entered our hands. Like most Manitobans I used to put the Free Press next the Bible and Eaton's catalogue, and thought I was safe both for here and the hereafter. I no longer look at the Free Press in that light; I look on it as the seller of the people's property in Manitoba. Mr. John Bracken was like a fly on the chariot wheel, and the Free Press was the chariot. I honour and respect our journalists, but these joint-stock companies with no conscience cannot be trusted with public opinion. This is the only place to mould public opinion, but we do not get a chance to do so. If we do not try to mould public opinion here; if we do not here try to bring our people to a sense of the value of what is theirs, there are other people on the outside who are doing their utmost to mislead the people.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has mentioned the power trust in the United States. A year ago this month the United States senate began an inquiry into the power trust of that country, and I have here some clippings taken at random, of which I will read only one from the Northwestern Christian Advocate:
The public utilities people have begun a practice which may become a menacing educational custom. According to facts recently brought to light by the federal trade commission, the utility interests have a huge financial interest in opposing the idea of government ownership. And they have gone at the business of opposing it with system, thoroughness and all the money they need.
They have paid out, in the last three years, a million a year to oppose government ownership-and how? By paying fees to men supposed to be impartial. By contributing, $30,000 to the General Federation of Women's Clubs for a "survey". By cooperating, financially and otherwise, with text-book writers, so as to get "bad books"'-that is, books favourable to public ownership-out of high schools and colleges, and "good books" in.
And by contributing sums large and small to colleges and universities for reports, lec-
	g
tures and inferentially for classroom instruction, on the merits of private, and the evils of public, ownership of public utilities.
Then I will add a little extract from a speech by Senator Norris, who said:
Recent developments by the federal trade commission have shown that there is a giant monopoly in the generation and distribution of electric current, gradually spreading itself over the entire country.
It has entered our schools and our homes. It has been working silently and stealthily to poison the minds of our school children. It has entered into the politics of the country from the school district to the White House. It has undertaken to buy seats in the United States Senate. It has made an attempt to control ail the avenues of publicity.
It has even reached its fingers into the church and undertaken to subsidize the men who preach to us from the pulpit on the Sabbath day.
All this came from an official investigation which took place less than a year ago. Organs such as the Free Press will say that we are not like that in Canada, that there is no earthly possibility that the stamp of men we have in Canada will permit that sort of thing to happen. My faith in Canadians is very deep and sincere, but I think we are of no different clay from our brethern to the south ; I believe we are just as susceptible to the almighty power of massed dollars as they are. As soon as it is worth while for the power trusts in that country and this-there is no difference between them- to poison the wells of knowledge and shape the plastic minds of our children to their own doctrines of private ownership and private greed they will do so. There is nothing here which we can do to prevent it; we have denied ourselves the means of preventing it and have closed up the only means of counteracting that poisonous propaganda.
A motion of this kind is highly reasonable; to permit this state of affairs to continue is not good for the people and is not good for the government. There is not one of us here who is not sorry for what has happened in Manitoba; that kind of happening cannot be good for Canada, when governments get trapped in that way and are held up to the contempt of their opponents and of public opinion generally. That cannot be good for Canada, but what was the vicious source of this sort of thing? It lay simply in this outworn system of disposing of our natural resources in the secrecy of a cabinet council. We did think Mr. Bracken sufficiently enlightened so that nothing would prevent him from consulting the people, but he stooped to tradition; he said, "No, this thing is our prerogative and we will settle it behind closed

Natural Resources-Mr. Bird
doors. The people of Manitoba and the people of Canada have no right to look in or protest." I think it most remarkable that Mr. Bracken and his colleagues should have absolutely ignored his friends in this house who, from the very beginning of last session, long before we knew what his policy was, set our hands against this transaction. Petitions were sent to the Minister of the Interior asking that these falls be retained for the public, yet Mr. Bracken and his colleagues went on with their secret negotiations with the Winnipeg Electric Company as though the representatives here did not exist or, if they did exist, their opinions were not worth while. These things discourage and astonish me; one sometimes wonders whether there is a spark of hope for any progress in our public life at all.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I know it will be said of the last speaker and myself that we display a regrettable suspiciousness in regard to our fellow human beings. That has been said already this session; I recall a reference made with regard to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), who said:
When my hon. friend suggests that the time may come when the banks will have been reduced in number to one, I say that he shows little confidence, little faith in the integrity of the public men of this country in believing that there could ever sit in the great office of Minister of Finance any man who would countenance an amalgamation or a merger unless it were in the interests of the depositors and to prevent raids upon the public treasury.
That utterance of the leader of the opposition was dictated, as I judge, purely by hi3 inborn disposition to preach sermons to other people. Where else did that criticism arise? Here is a gentleman who is drawing a salary to criticize the government; the very logic of his position is that the government cannot be trusted in the way he says it ought to be: Where else can criticism of the government come from except from the official opposition? That is rightly so; but why should we be marked when we express distrust of the government? Is that not the very basis of the development of our British institutions? Do not public men accept it that their whole conduct will be submitted to the clear light of reason? Surely they do; that is the foundation of our parliamentary system. When I seem to cast doubt upon the Bracken government, or upon this government, I must say that I rather hesitate. It is not a popular thing to do, especially with the governments that have been criticized. But on the other hand, here are the people of Manitoba whom I must put in the balance against those who have arrogated to themselves the right to 7S594-29
dispose of the people's natural wealth. It may be against my disposition to cast unjustifiable reflections upon the government, or upon the Minister of the Interior, and I do not go as far as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) went. The Minister of the Interior did say to us quite plainly, before we left for home last session, that he could not hold up this matter until the Manitoba legislature met; he was very frank about that. But if I did not misunderstand him, and there is always the possibility that I might have-I can confirm what I am saying by my own diary, and his words in the house seem to confirm it-he said that before anything was done the members for Manitoba would be consulted. As I say, there may have been misunderstanding, and it is a very critical situation in which to make a mistake, but if the Minister of the Interior draws upon himself widespread suspicion he cannot blame those who are the instruments of diverting it upon him; he can blame only himself for the inconsecutive way in which he carried on his negotiations with us. We representatives of Manitoba had a natural right to expect that he would consult us, not personally but with respect to the position we hold as federal members for Manitoba. We all signed a round robin on the 4th of February 'last saying that the Seven Sisters falls must be kept for the people of Manitoba, and not one Manitoba member withheld his name from that document.

speechtext:
I think I can state to the house that I very rarely make statements unless I am sure of their truth; I always do the house the honour of addressing it only when I am fairly well prepared.
As I said, we started out in Manitoba on new lines, as we thought, politically. I am almost ashamed of the number of platforms on which I stood and said, "here is the real thing in party politics." I think I was the only federal member in Manitoba who supported the Bracken government last year. I think I was the only federal member who went out and stood four-square for Mr. Bracken. What had I to say for Mr. Bracken and his government? I said, "here are men who do not say one thing and do another." I said that on every platform in my constituency, and I have made everlasting enemies of some of my supporters.
This is a serious situation, not only for me but for all those who believe that the pursuit of idealism is possible in public life, who believe there can be found an aggregation of men who will go to the country and say, "Here is what we will do if we get into power,"-and mean it. That is the message we had from Vancouver to Halifax in 1921. Mr. Crerar carried the banner of pure politics from one end of the country to the other, and he found an echo in thousands of hearts. But the people now ask if this is the same government they supported in 1922, the government that pledged itself to retain the water-powers for public ownership and then turned around and deliberately handed them over to private interests in a secret session.
It is not an easy matter for me to say the things I have said in the last few sentences, because I have committed myself in the last few years to the notion that idealism is possible in all the ramifications of public life. Some of us have not come into politics of our own intiative: we came from walks of life where we had no ambitions whatsoever, and we were brought into public life with the thought that the avocation we had been following would somehow be a guarantee that through all our public career we would 3tand four-square for idealism in public life. But how are we going to hold up our heads 
again when we remember what has happened in Manitoba during the last few months? How are we going to go on the platforms in our constituencies and face the finger of scorn from every quarter? All these petty things do not count much with the rising generation in the west. It was appealed to in 1922 in Manitoba, not respecting things of petty policy but as regards things that lay deeper down than political policies. Some of us have been called Don Quixotes, and I do not accept that altogether as a criticism; I have gladly tilted at windmills during the last twelve months, especially in my own constituency. Men who were my strong friends, went on one side while I was on the other. The past president of my own political organization to-night is on one side with private ownership, and I with public ownership. Who is to blame? We say: the Bracken government. I have said: the Free Press. I do not know perhaps whether we are justified in saying this or that, but some weakness has crept in somewhere. There has been some blurring of those clean-cut ideas with which some of us came here a few years ago. There has been some giving way, some unconscious forsaking of things we stood for then. I say it with sorrow more than with anger, that somehow or another I have the feeling of being forsaken, not only by the Manitoba government, but in a measure by the federal government, although the federal government, as far as I know, never committed itself to public ownership, and to that extent perhaps, it escapes criticism.

Just give me an opportunity to explain. What I mean is that I am not convinced that all the virtue lies in public ownership nor am I convinced that all the virtue lies in private ownership. I occupy a position where I think I have a fair chance to observe the working out of both systems of handling the public domain, or, if you will, the natural resources. Ontario is making a success of hydro; in Quebec, they appear to be making a success of it under private ownership; at least that is the decision of the government and people of Quebec. They are just as convinced they are on the right track in regard to private ownership as are the people of Ontario in regard to public ownership. The same thing applies to British Columbia and to the maritime provinces. Ontario, although it has hydro, is issuing leases for mines, timbers and water powers and is issuing them by order in council just as this government is doing. Under the direction of the Minister of Mines or whatever minister is in charge, the administration of the natural resources of the provinces is being carried out in this particular way. I claim no virtue, but I challenge my hon. friend or any other hon. member to say that I have not consulted to a greater degree in every respect hon. members who represent the various provinces than are private members of any of the provinces consulted about the issuing of leases in their respective provinces. I have always done that and I challenge my hon. friend again to name any lease of any importance that meant any-

speechtext:
Will my hon. friend give me a chance? He has made some rather scathing assertions with respect to my administration, and I propose to deal with them before I get through.
My hon. friend states that in so far as this particular lease is concerned, it should have been preserved in the public interest. May I just rehearse what has happened with respect to this particular lease? My position has never changed; I believe the lease is a good one. I said so to my hon. friend in my office; I said so to him on many occasions, as well as to other members representing the province of Manitoba; I say so still. I believe it is in the public interest, and I will give the house some of my reasons for saying so.
I have nothing to do with the action of the Manitoba government. I do not know anything about it; I do not know anything about what happened to them or why they are in difficulties to-day. I simply make the statement that I have not changed my mind about this lease, and I still believe it is in the public interest.
If my hon. friend will go back some years -I shall not have time to deal with details- he will remember that the Winnipeg Electric Company was established at Pinawa Falls, on a diversion from the Winnipeg river proper. This government has gone to very considerable trouble to secure for the people of Manitoba and for the city of Winnipeg a complete utilization of the power on the Winnipeg river, and that has not been done without a good deal of controversy. It has not been done without having parted me at least from some of my strongest and warmest political friends in that province who differed with me. I shall not have time to cover the whole details of what happened, but many of the older members of this house will remember the controversy about the Norman dam and as to the preservation of the levels of the lake of the Woods, and in respect to storage facilities in lac Seul in Ontario, to assist power development on the Winnipeg river. Hon. members will remember that there was a good deal of controversy about that.

I do not know anything about the history of the Winnipeg Electric Company. I do not know how they treated the people of Manitoba. They may have treated them very .badly for all I know I do not know anything about the history of the company, but they were established at Pinawa long before I had anything to do with the administration of this department. We were anxious in our scheme for the development of the Winnipeg watershed to scrap the plant on the Pinawa diversion and throw the whole flowage of the river over to the Seven Sisters development, thereby securing for the people of Manitoba and for the city of Winnipeg fifty thousand home power more than could be developed if the Pinajwa plant were continued in operation. That was our first reason.
The Winnipeg Electric Company made first application for the development of the Seven Sisters falls. Later on when the controversy was on with respect to the Manitoba pulp and paper mill, my hon. friends will remember the bombardment to which I was subjected on that occasion, and I want to say again that the Manitoba members stood by me and gave me advice that was very valuable to me, and I think I shall be able to prove that they gave me good advice in connection with this matter. The Backus interests wished to secure this power site, and' my hon. friends will remember that that application was backed up by very strong support from the city of Winnipeg, because they were promised a pulp mill there. I did not believe we were in a position at that time to warrant the application for a second pulp mill in the province of Manitoba, and I think later events have proved that my judgment on that occasion was sound. Nor did I think they were entitled to get the water power until such time as we were able to say to them that there was a possibility for development in the pulp and paper industry. They did not get it.
Later on, in 1925, Mr. Bracken became interested in this power site. I am led to believe from what my hon. friend has said, and particularly from what he has said about the Free Press, that someone must have been interested in the Manitoba government securing power rights in Manitoba for operation as a public utility. Mr. Bracken came to me and said that he was desirous of obtaining this power site. I have heard it stated that I had something to do with guiding Mr. Bracken in this matter. I never did. I make that assertion most fully and completely. I said to him, "Mr. Bracken," as I would say to the province of Alberta or to the province

Natural Resources-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
of Saskatchewan, "if you are desirous of having any of these water-powers and developing them as a public utility for the benefit of the people, then your application will be given priority over all comers." That was the assurance Mr. Bracken got from me on behalf of the federal government, and he occupied that position for almost eighteen months or more. But I made this statement. 1 said, "Mr. Bracken, in order to have full development on the Winnipeg river, we are desirous of getting rid of that Pinawa plant and throwing the whole flowage over the Seven Sisters falls, in order that we may have a larger power development than could be obtained by a division of these two interests." That was the only suggestion I made to the Premier of Manitoba. Not only that-and I must thank my hon. friend for reading the resolution passed by the members of the assembly for Manitoba, in which they pointed out that in the event of the province of Manitoba or the city of Winnipeg not requiring this public development, then they had no objection- in other words, no objection to placing the Winnipeg Electric in a position of priority.

I am coming to that; I want to deal with it in sequence. That was the resolution my hon. friend has read, and with which I agree.
The only condition I made was that Mr. Bracken take upon himself the responsibility of seeing whether or not it would be possible to make an arrangement with the Winnipeg Electric for the scrapping of that plant and diverting the whole flowage down the river. I want to make it clear that I did not put any strings on it, and state to Mr. Bracken what would result if he was not able to do that. I said I hoped he would try to do that in the interests of securing more power for Manitoba or the full utilization of the power available. If he had not been able to do that, there would have been no hesitancy on my part in recommending that the license should be issued to him. He went on and made an arrangement with the Winnipeg Electric. He had time to call in men in whom he had confidence, and men in whom I had the utmost confidence-particularly Doctor Hogg of the Ontario Hydro. I have worked with Doctor Hogg on the Niagara, and on other power and scenic developments, and he is a man whose opinion I value very highly. I did not see Doctor
Hogg's report till long afterwards, but in effect Doctor Hogg advised Mr. Bracken, after viewing the whole situation, and having in mind the requirements of the province of Manitoba-the provincial government could not hope to dispose of any power to the city of Winnipeg, because it already had a development. The city had already made application for the Slave Falls, which they are now to develop, in order to supplement the power they already have. I make no defence of Mr. Bracken; I am simply stating the facts. He had no hope of selling power to the city of Winnipeg. His sales would be confiened to the rural parts, and in his arrangement he provided, first, for the scrapping of the Pinawa plant, carrying out what we were desirous of having done; secondly, he was to get for his own service thirty thousand horse-power for a period of thirty years, at a price in the neighbourhood of twelve dollars per horsepower.

Now, what about public ownership? I had very clear evidence so far as the province

was concerned from the men who I thought represented Manitoba-the provincial government-that they did not require the power. They had had their chance. I took the precaution to ascertain whether or not the city of Winnipeg was interested. I could not find that it was. The city was interested in securing Slave falls, and stated that for some years it would be developing that power site, and at the moment it was not interested in the development of this power. That is my defence, Mr. Speaker, with respect to what my hon. friends have repeatedly said, that if there was a demand by the public to develop this property they should have their chance. They did have their chance; they refused that chance, and asked me to issue the lease to the power company.
Dealing with what my hon. friend has said as to my not having kept my word with respect to this matter, it is quite true that time and again I consulted the Manitoba members about this very matter. It is quite true that several of them, like the two hon. gentlemen who have spoken and possibly some others who will speak, have never changed their minds on the advantages of public ownership versus private ownership in connection with this matter. It is not true that I did not consult the Manitoba members. My hon. friend said I did not see him. Well, I made an attempt to see him, but he was not in the province, neither was the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). With respect to my hon. friend from Nelson (Mr. Bird), I was not able to see him, but on two occasions I did see a goodly number of the other members from Manitoba.
Now then, let me say this. In July, in accordance with the agreement with the Manitoba government, Premier Bracken came to Ottawa. I think he arrived on July 3, because I know on the night of the fourth 1 left for western Canada. I spent the day with Premier Bracken and the members of our government discussing the possibility of the transfer of the natural resources to the province. On that occasion there was a good deal of discussion as to what I might term new demands 'by the provincial authorities. The next day also was spent in discussion.
I was not present. After this discussion an agreement was drawn up which provided, amongst other things, that a commission should be appointed to study the whole question of placing Manitoba on an equality with the other provinces of Canada as from the date of her creation as a province. It was also arranged that pending the report by the commission and the transfer of these resources, they were to be administered in

accordance with the wishes of the provincial government. That happened, I imagine, on July 5. On July 4 I -was not present, but I assume that that was the agreement which was entered into between our government and the government of Manitoba.
That agreement included all of the natural resources. When I visited Manitoba later I interviewed many of the federal members from the province and discussed the matter with them. After considerable discussion it was agreed that so far as the Seven Sisters power site was concerned-for I felt I owed some obligation to the Manitoba members to discuss it with them-if the provincial government were to take the responsibility of advising that this power site should be given to a private company, then the best thing for the government of Canada to do was to hand this development over direct to the Manitoba government. That was done by me after returning to Ottawa in a letter addressed to the premier of the province some time early in September. He replied stating that he could not accept the resources in that manner.

speechtext:
What I want to point out is that if there was unanimity on one occasion it has not continued throughout even this session. Now, feeling as I did that as a government, myself being the minister in charge, we had some responsibility to the government of Manitoba, after having agreed with them that we should administer these resources according to their wishes, naturally when the government of Manitoba were insistent I was taking all the precautions I could to protect the public interest. I would do so in any case, and until the time when the lease itself was issued late in September we took these precautions to safeguard the public. The company is not the Winnipeg Electric Company; it is the Northwestern Company, a separate entity altogether from the Winnipeg Electric; and our object was to separate this unit of construction from any other. In any construction of this character we put an engineer in charge. In this case the agreement provides that if the engineer in charge and the company's engineers do not agree with regard to construction costs then the matter shall be referred to the court for decision, and the court's decision fixes the actual price of the work. Let me be clear about that: it does not fix the price of the transmission lines, but of the works, the transmission lines being supervised by the Dominion government's engineer. The price is fixed by that engineer, but if there is a disagreement between the company and him, then the actual price is fixed by reference to the exchequer court. Why did we so provide? We did so in order to avoid just the things that have been pointed out by my hon. friend; We wished to see that undue costs were not entailed in construction, and we also had in view later on putting in the hands of the board of public utilities, or of the minister himself if he so desires, the fixing of rates for the protection of the public. In that event the minister would know exactly what the undertaking would cost.
Moreover, there is provision in the contract that the government of Manitoba may take over the enterprise at the end of thirty years on the same valuation, less depreciation; they may acquire it after the plant has been operated for thirty years. Of course, the lease itself runs fifty years, but if it is taken over at the end of thirty years provision is made for compensation to the company; it is definitely and clearly provided that a certain percentage will.be paid on the unexpired term, but the provincial government may acquire the undertaking as I have stated. In the meantime, every interest of the public is protected in so far as inflation and false returns with respect to costs are concerned.
456	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
That protection is thrown around the construction of this work. And the same precaution is taken not only in this connection but in every other work of this character; with respect to the very work which is going on at the present time in the constituency of the leader of the opposition in West Calgary, the Calgary Power Company are constructing a large power plant and the same procedure is being followed. Provision is made that control of rates may be had by the Minister of the Interior, but preferably by the public utilities board of the province in which the utility is to be operated. That is provided for. Provision is also made for the acquisition of the plant at the end of the thirty year period, at a fixed price; and until the price is fixed no operating license is issued. In this case they are constructing on an interim license, the license to be issued only after we have agreed upon the price.
I do not know of a single provision omitted from this contract which would protect the public interest; if there is any such omission I should be glad to know what it is. I know it is an easy thing to say that there will be inflation and that there is no redress against the rapacity of a private corporation. Let me say however that I have tried to provide against anything of the sort ever since I have had the honour to administer the natural resources under my department; I have endeavoured to guard against that very thing.
I wish once more to make it clear that I gave the province of Manitoba every opportunity to develop the enterprise; I gave the city of Winnipeg that opportunity. And the city of Winnipeg has the Slave falls. I believe we are getting, by the procedure which we are following, the full possible development on the Winnipeg river for the people of Manitoba, and we are safeguarding the public of that province against undue rates. May I add this: Not only did I want to be sure of my position with the Manitoba government, but you will find by reference to the documents that I insisted that there should be no mistake about the matter. The Manitoba government passed an order in council authorizing the issue of the lease to the Manitoba Power Company. This order in council was passed on September 11, 1928, and at the meeting there were present: The Hon. Mr. Bracken; Mr. McLeod; Mr. Prefontaine; Mr. Hoey; Mr. Montgomery.

I have shown that the resolution does not deal with power sites but with all the natural resources, and how impossible it would be to administer the natural resources as outlined in this resolution. I have no quarrel with my hon. friends with respect to their advocacy of public ownership, but I do say that in fairness to the contract itself and in fairness to the development of the Winnipeg river, so far as .the protection of public interest is concerned no such public interest has been neglected. The machinery is all there for the regulations of rates; means are taken to provide for a guarantee that there will be no excessive costs entering construction; machinery is provided for the acquisition of this undertaking by the province, if they wish to do so, at a valuation fixed in the contract itself.
