speakeroldname: Hon R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition) :
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution moved

Natural Resources-Mr. Bennett
by the hon. gentleman whose address we heard, the speech made by the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) and the reply of the minister raise a question of some considerable importance. I have not time to-night to do more than direct attention to rather an important phase of it which has been dwelt upon by the minister. I take it that this house is not concerned with whether or not Manitoba made a good bargain; that is a matter for the electors of the province of Manitoba to settle, but to the extent to which this government became a party to a transaction which may merit public condemnation-whether or not it does I am not saying at the moment-is a matter for the consideration of parliament.
It must be borne in mind that the province of Manitoba has been endeavouring to secure its resources for a number of years, and what has a very strange aspect is that on July 3 and 4 last, only a few days after the prorogation of this parliament the Premier ot the province of Manitoba discussed this question with the government of the day, and an announcement was made on July 11, 1928, as follows:
Following a conference held at Ottawa on July 3 and 4, 1928, between representatives of the government of Canada and of the government of Manitoba, the results of which conference have since been approved by the two governments, agreement was reached as to the method and basis of settlement of the question of the administration and control of the natural resources of Manitoba, as follows:-
1.	The province of Manitoba to be placed in a position of equality with the other provinces of confederation with respect to the administration and control of its natural resources, as from its entrance into confederation in 1870.
2.	The government of Canada, with the concurrence of the government of Manitoba, to appoint a commission of three persons to enquire and report as to what financial readjustments should be made to effect this end.
3.	The commission to be empowered to decide what financial or other considerations are relevant to its enquiry.
4.	The findings of the commission to be submitted to the parliament of Canada and to the legislature of Manitoba.
5.	Upon agreement on the financial terms following consideration of the report of the commission, the respective governments to introduce the necessary legislation to give effect to the financial terms as agreed upon, and to effect the transfer to the province of the unalienated natural resources within its boundaries, subject to any trust existing in respect thereof, and without prejudice to any interest other than that of the crown in the same.
6.	Pending this transfer, the policy of the government of Canada in the administration of the natural resources of Manitoba to be in accord with wishes of the government of the province.
It must be remembered that notwithstanding the years during which continuous efforts
were made by the successive governments of Manitoba to conclude their dealings with this Dominion, and the fact that the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were not able to conclude their dealings with this government, suddenly on July 11 this announcement was made, that the agreement had been negotiated on July 3 and 4 between the government of Manitoba and the government of Canada. Why was Manitoba thus singled out? Did that fact bear any relation to the fact that during a period of months efforts had been made to alienate a power site, which efforts had failed up to that time because the members of this parliament from the province of Manitoba had filed a protest against action being taken by this government? That is the question we must consider, and it will be borne in mind further that on June 6, less than a month before action was taken to turn over the resources to the province of Manitoba, the minister made a statement in answer to a question put by myself, in which I said:
My submission is that sinice we hold these resources, that is, they are the property of the crown in the right of the Dominion, in trust for the crown in the right of the several provinces, we should not as an executive act or as a pure matter of administration part with so valuable a resource as a power site which is of such inestimable value to the people of the country, without the approval of this parliament. In my judgment that would be a proper release to the minister for any action he might take as trustee for the people affected, and would afford an opportunity to the several legislatures to deal with any matter which concerned them until such time as these resources, notably the power sites, ivere turned over to the crown in the right of the several provinces concerned.
At page 3853 of Hansard for last year the Minister of the Interior, who is the present minister, said:
May I give my hon. friend the assurance now that so far as his request is concerned I have no serious objection to offer except this: Of course I am always made more or less the storm centre for the settlement of these difficulties, particularly in Manitoba, but I have adopted the principle of consulting with the provincial governments about these matters. Possibly I have carried that principle too far, but I am never forgetful of the fact that I must take the responsibility for final disposition. I am going to say very frankly here and now that notwithstanding the fact that at present the government have adopted a line of action with respect to the Seven Sister falls I am not in any particular hurry to come to any decision about that matter, largely because of the fact that the members of this house have expressed very decided opinions about the matter as federal members. I am not very much disturbed by the statement that there must be immediate action; I have investigated the matter pretty well and I think there is plenty of time to give ample consideration to this matter before it is decided. In order to settle the
458	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. Bennett
question, and in order to prevent any delay, I do not see any reason why we should not await the action of the city council of Winnipeg and of the provincial government, which must take the responsibility, before a final decision is made here. I think that should satisfy my hon. friend.
II put this to the minister: Why was it that in a few short weeks the matter became so urgent that, in order to keep faith with the language he used in parliament, all the natural resources were turned over to the province of Manitoba? Why was it that Alberta was not so considered, and why was not Saskatchewan dealt with in this way also? Why were not the resources of Alberta turned over under a formal agreement without regard to nicety of terms or details? Why was it that the Premier of Saskatchewan came here the other day in this connection and was unable to make a bargain? With respect to Manitoba the only bargain made was to say that the Dominion would turn over the resources to Manitoba just as though it was one of the older provinces, and would account for them since 1870 when Manitoba was formed. Why could not that be done with respect to Alberta and Saskatchewan?

It is all right to talk about taking steps for the purpose of safeguarding the public interests of the people of Manitoba, but the people of Manitoba are capable of doing that themselves. The trouble with this
whole matter throughout Manitoba and throughout Canada is that no one has yet been able to understand why the minister made the statement that was made on the 6th day of June last, as to the position taken by this government, when there was no hurry, and that the city of Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba would be consulted; and then within thirty days after the house rose these resources are all transferred, so far as this government is concerned, by an agreement subject only to the question of accounting. The minister said, "We will administer them as the province of Manitoba want us to," but that is not what we were discussing. That is not -the attitude this parliament took; that is not the attitude the members from Manitoba took when they communicated with this house; that is not what was contained in the round robin presented to the minister, according to the gentleman who presented it. Why this unseemly haste? Why this sudden hurry? Why this sudden scurrying to and fro to settle a question of resources which had been engaging the attention of statesmen in this country for the last thirty years? Why is Manitoba treated one way and Alberta another? That is the question, and it is one to which this country is going to have an answer.

speechtext:
So far as
each province is concerned, we are perfectly willing to try to deal with them on the basis on which they will negotiate with us, always having in mind the federal intersts.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman say that that was the case from the very day the Liberal party first changed their minds in denying our resources; from the day the minister himself heard his then leader in the legislature of Alberta pass a resolution that we demand our resources; from the day that Mr. Sifton sent his letter to Sir Wilfrid Laurier? Was there ever a time when the province of Alberta has not said, all we want is our resources with an accounting since 1870?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Not since
1870; since 1905.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: The speech by Mr. Haul-tain made in the old Territorial legislature when I was present; the speeches in the legislature of Alberta when Mr. Sifton was the leader, and in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, have all been a demand for one thing, and one thing only: that we should have our resources as they stand with an accounting from the time we became part of Canada up to the date of the accounting being made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: And a subsidy.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I cannot be taken away from the point; the subsidy had nothing to do with it.	.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Has my hon. friend the letter written by Mr. Arthur Sifton? It did not make any demand for an accounting.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: He demanded that compensation should be given for the resources which had been alienated before we became a province.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will look up the letter I think he will
change his mind.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Let us not get away from the question. Why the haste? Why the hurry? Do not let us get away for a single moment from the question that is agitating the people.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, February 26, 1929
